# The BRRRR method in Myrtle Beach: bank-owned houses about 17 percent under market.
By Devin Day , Operations Officer · Chapter3 Realty · Updated November 1, 2026
BRRRR uses one pool of capital to buy rental after rental. The Horry County math: bank-owned houses about 17 percent under market, and the refinance that returns your cash.

The strategy

## The BRRRR method: one sum of cash, reused house after house
BRRRR means buy, rehab, rent, refinance, repeat: one sum of cash, reused house after house. You buy a worn, outdated house cheap, fix it, rent it, then refinance to pull your cash back out . The two boxes below give you the ten-second read on whether it fits you. BRRRR is the scarcest strategy we work on the Grand Strand, because the right house is rare, and finding it is most of what Chapter3 does for a BRRRR investor.
Why people do it

- + The same cash buys house after house

- + Rent covers the new loan

- + You keep the house and the rent

What can go wrong

- ! The house appraises low and your cash stays stuck

- ! The rehab runs over budget

- ! The rent does not cover the new loan payment

The five steps

## How BRRRR works, step by step

- 1 Buy below market. Pay a price that leaves room after repairs.

- 2 Rehab it. Fix what raises the value and the rent.

- 3 Rent it. A signed lease is what the refinance lender wants to see.

- 4 Refinance: pull your cash back out. A new loan on the higher value hands most of your cash back.

- 5 Repeat with the same cash. The money you pulled out buys the next house.

The buy

## Buying below market, where the rent is strong
Aim to keep the purchase price plus rehab budget under 70 to 75 percent of the after-repair value, what the house will be worth once it is fixed up. That difference is what covers you if the work costs more than planned.
The house also has to sit where rent is strong. BRRRR pays you back through a refinance, and that loan is judged on the rent the house collects, so a cheap house on a street with weak rent does not work. Needing both in the same house is what makes these deals scarce.
On the Grand Strand, dated single-family homes in Conway, Socastee and Carolina Forest are the usual targets, and the map runs north through Longs and Little River, where prices drop again. Year-round tenant s keep the rent side steady.

Sourcing

## Where the discounted houses come from
Bank-owned listings are the usual starting point. A bank that has taken a house back sells it for less than a fixed-up house nearby, and that discount is what the strategy runs on. By our own tracking of sales, bank-owned houses have sold about 17.34 percent under market value on average. The buyer who can close soonest usually gets the house.
The same tracking puts distressed condo units at about 22.32 percent under market, the deeper discount because condo supply is larger and many investors will not buy into a building at all. Estate sales and worn rentals coming off long tenancies make up the rest.
We hear about bank-owned and pre-listing houses early, from agents who have worked this market for decades, and our analysts screen every active listing for rent-to-price math at the same time.

Condos

## Buying a distressed condo unit
Distressed condo units in stable buildings sell at deeper discounts than houses, because the supply of condos is bigger and many investors will not buy into a building at all. The discount usually comes from the owner, not the building: one mismanaged or foreclosing unit sells cheap while the building itself still passes lender tests.
A building that fails those tests is called non-warrantable. The lenders who will still refinance you there want about 25 percent down, against the 20 percent a warrantable building can take, so another 5 percent of the value stays parked in that unit instead of funding your next purchase. Figures from BrickWood Mortgage.
Our agents check the building before you offer. The full picture is on the condotel and non-warrantable condo financing guide .

The work

## The rehab, the lease, and how we help
Fix what raises the value and the rent, not a wish list. Our agents walk the house with you before you offer and tell you which repairs the appraiser and the tenant will pay for, and which ones you will never get back. We introduce the contractors we use here, so the bids come from people who have done this work on the Grand Strand.
Once the work is done, a signed lease is what the refinance lender wants to see. Inland areas lease fastest. Demand there comes from workers, hospitals, schools and Coastal Carolina University , not tourists. Houses approved for the housing choice voucher program lease fastest of all, and we walk owners through what the housing authority inspects and how to get a unit approved.
One local rehab for scale: a house on Woodlawn Drive took $90,317.80 of work from a local company we recommend. A new roof, replaced rotted studs, new insulation, new cabinets, counters and backsplashes, repaired floors and walls, fresh paint, and a hot tub for short-term guests. The house was worth about $180,000 before the work and appraised at $384,000 after, and BrickWood Mortgage financed the project with no money down. Start to finish, financing included, about three months, and the buyer kept it as a short-term rental. His numbers, not a promise.

The refinance

## The refinance that returns your cash
The new loan is usually a DSCR cash-out loan: the loan qualifies on the property's rent, not your tax returns. Most lenders cap the cash-out at 75 to 80 percent of the new appraised value. Many also require seasoning, meaning the lender makes you wait a few months before using the new value. Our lending partner skips seasoning for BRRRR investors here, so your cash comes back months sooner. See the DSCR loan guide for how the refinance works.
When an appraisal does come in low, and here that is rare, our agents pull their own comparable sales from the Coastal Carolinas MLS and file a reconsideration of value through the lender. In the past, one of those changed the number, and the borrower brought less cash to closing.

The repeat

## Doing it again with the same money
If the after-repair value holds, most of your cash is back and the tenant covers the loan. If the house appraises under the number the deal was priced on, your cash stays stuck in it. Pricing that number is the part our agents do with you before you buy, from sold homes nearby rather than from an estimate.
Tim's grandfather owned rental property in Horry County, and Tim owns rentals here today, so the numbers Chapter3 runs for you are the numbers he runs on his own investments. Run the rent and value numbers through the long-term rental analyzer before you buy. If you would rather sell the finished house than keep it, that is a fix and flip . Read that guide to see whether it suits you better.

Another way in

## The new construction version of BRRRR
The scarce ingredient is the discounted house. One way around it is to create the value instead of shopping for it. We work with a local builder whose built houses appraised for more than they cost to build, and a brand new house rents higher than a comparable older one .
The rent side gets solved during the build. We look for tenants moving to the area around the month the house will be finished, so about nine times in ten the house has a renter lined up before the work ends. The cycle is the same as BRRRR, with the discount coming from the build rather than from a distressed seller.
One house took about $260,000 of capital to build, half of it financed, and appraised at $390,000 once it was done. Those are his numbers, not a promise. This path needs a builder relationship or a real discount during construction, so it is not open to every investor. Ask us whether your numbers fit it.

Paying cash

## Benefits of buying cash
A cash offer is stronger than a financed one on these houses. Bank-owned and off-market houses are the first two places our agents look, and both usually go to the buyer who can close soonest. Cash has no appraisal to fail and no loan to fall through, which is worth more to those sellers than a slightly higher price.
Cash does not have to stay in the house either. The refinance step is the same one BRRRR already runs: buy with cash, fix it, sign a lease, then take a DSCR cash-out loan and put the money back to work. Our lending partner skips the waiting period on that refinance, so the cash comes back sooner than most investors expect.
You can still buy these houses with a loan, and off-market is where it happens, because there is no competing cash offer to lose to. Our agents talk to owners before a house is listed and find out what the seller needs. Then we build the offer around it: the closing date they want, a shorter inspection window, more earnest money, or a price that pays them for waiting on your loan. A seller who has not listed yet is usually weighing one offer instead of five, and that is the situation where financing wins.

Common questions

## Frequently asked questions

### Does the BRRRR method work in Myrtle Beach?
Yes. It works best on dated single-family homes in inland areas like Conway, Socastee, Carolina Forest, and up toward Longs and Little River. Year-round tenant demand there supports the rent side. Distressed condo units sell at deeper discounts, but HOA rules limit what you can renovate and many oceanfront buildings fail refinance lender tests, so check the building against the refinance before you buy.

### What is the 70 percent rule in BRRRR?
It is a guideline. Keep the purchase price plus rehab budget under about 70 to 75 percent of the fixed-up value. That margin is what lets you refinance later and pull most of your cash back out.

### How soon can I refinance a BRRRR property?
Many lenders require seasoning, meaning they make you wait a few months before lending on the new value. Our preferred lender does not require seasoning for BRRRR investors, so there is no waiting period. That makes the after-repair value the deciding number. The refinance comes down to what the house appraises for once the work is done. Know the house, its condition, and what similar homes nearby sold for before you buy. That is what protects your cash.

### How much cash can I pull out on the refinance?
Cash-out DSCR refinances are typically capped at 75 to 80 percent of the appraised value. Whether you recover all of your cash depends on how accurate your fixed-up value estimate was.

### What is the biggest risk with BRRRR?
Guessing the fixed-up value too high. If the house appraises low, the refinance returns less cash and more of your money stays stuck. Model the value and rent before you buy.

# How do you find a fix and flip in Myrtle Beach? What quick resales gained here last year, where they were, and how our deal finder looks for the next one.
By Devin Day , Operations Officer · Reviewed by Tim Nash , Broker-in-Charge · Updated October 29, 2026
Local numbers from the county's deeds, the 70 percent rule, and the rules a flip meets here.

The short answer
Yes, a fix and flip can pay here if you buy right. In the year to September 2026, Horry County homes were resold within 12 months of their last sale at least 344 times. When a company resold the home, the middle gain between the two deed prices was about $75,000, before any costs. Conway, Carolina Forest and Little River had the biggest gains on houses.
Our deal finder pulls every house for sale with a reason to be cheap and compares it with what houses its size sold for nearby. An agent then reads the repairs and works out your highest offer.

## Do fix and flips make money in Myrtle Beach?
Most resell for more than the earlier deed price. We read every deed Horry County recorded for two years. Quick resales, a home sold again within 12 months of its last sale, were about 3 of every 100 home sales not made by a builder. The chart gives the middle gain: half gained more, half less.
Middle gain on a home resold within 12 months, Horry County Who resold it, how many middle gain

Resold by a company · about 140 resales $75,000
Every quick resale · 344 resales $38,000
Resold by a person · about 200 resales $15,000

The gain between the two deed prices, before repairs, loans, taxes, insurance and both closings. Resales recorded in the 12 months to September 2026. The count is a floor: some sales that may have been a lot that became a new house were left out.
The company figure is the closer guide to an investor's flip. Resales by a person hold most of the losses: about 55 of the 66 homes that sold for less than the earlier deed price. Houses also gained more than condos, a middle of about $56,000 against about $17,000.

## Where on the Grand Strand do flips happen?
The biggest gains on houses were in Conway, Carolina Forest and Little River. Myrtle Beach had the most quick resales, but most were condos, and the middle one gained about $22,000. No single neighborhood had more than three house resales: the flips are spread across many streets. The deal finder looks at every home for sale for that reason.

## How do we find a house worth flipping?
Our agents use a deal finder we built to look at every home for sale on the Grand Strand in one pass. An agent checks everything it finds:

- A reason to be cheap. It pulls every house for sale that has one: a distressed sale, a foreclosure , a short sale, or an older house at the low end of the price range.

- The nearby sales. For the cheapest houses per square foot, it finds houses of about the same size that sold within a mile in the last year.

- The list. The houses furthest under the middle of their nearby sales make the list. It reads the photos and description of the top ones and lists the repairs it can see, with a cost range for each.

- The agent's call. An agent reads the sales, decides what the house will sell for once it is fixed, and works out your highest offer. That number comes from an agent who knows the streets, never from a computer.

A house far under its neighbors is not always a deal. Sometimes the size in the listing is wrong, the price is an auction's opening bid, or the house needs everything. The finder marks those, and the agent finds out which it is before you spend a dollar.
What you get on the flip list
For each house: its asking price per square foot against the middle of its nearby sales, the six nearest sales, the repairs its photos show with a cost range, and your highest offer by the 70 percent rule. Tell us your price range.

## How do you work out what to offer?
Every flip starts with the after-repair value, what the house will sell for once it is fixed up. Take that number and subtract everything you spend. What is left is your profit.
Many flippers use the 70 percent rule to set their highest offer: 70 percent of the after-repair value, minus the repairs. On a house that will sell for $300,000 fixed up and needs $45,000 of work, that is $165,000. The 30 percent left over covers your costs and your profit.
Run your own deal
What it sells for fixed up $ What you pay $ Repairs $ Holding and selling costs $
Your profit $25,000
Price plus repairs, as a share of the fixed-up value 82%
Above the 70 percent most flippers aim for, so this deal leaves little room for the repairs to run over.

## What does a flip cost here besides the house and the repairs?
Four costs bill you every month you own the house: the property tax, the loan, insurance and utilities. The rest come at the two closings, and when you sell, the commission and the deed fee.
The tax is the one most investors miss. A house that is not its owner's own home is taxed on 6 percent of its value, not 4 percent, and it pays the school operating tax.
On a house the county appraises at $250,000, in one of its tax districts outside the cities, that is about $3,015 a year instead of about $919, plus an $89.40 fee on each bill. We work out the bill for the actual address, and every town's rate is in our property tax calculator .
The deed fee is $1.85 for each $500 of the price, and the law puts it on the seller: about $962 on a $260,000 sale. If you buy at the county's court-ordered foreclosure sale, you pay the fee on that deed as well.
We also get the insurance quotes for the empty house and the loan's terms, so the monthly cost of holding it is a number, not a guess.

## What permits and licenses does a flip need?
In Horry County outside the cities, you need a building permit to build, alter, repair or tear down, and for any electrical, gas, mechanical or plumbing work. South Carolina licenses the people who do the work by the size of the job:
Permits and licenses for flip work in Horry County The work County permit Who may do it
Paint, wallpaper, tile, carpet, cabinets, countertops No You, or a pro registered with the state
A new roof We check first A roofer registered with the state
Electrical, plumbing, heating and air Yes A contractor licensed for the trade
Walls, structure, a full renovation Yes A licensed builder, for jobs over $5,000

Before you budget a new roof, we ask the county's code office whether it needs a permit. The county's own pages disagree.
The owner's exemption from the license does not cover a flip. It is only for a house you build or repair to live in, and a sale or rental within two years of finishing is presumed to mean it was done to sell.
Working without the license is a misdemeanor for the contractor, with a fine of $500 to $10,000, at least 30 days in jail, or both. An unlicensed contractor also cannot put a lien on the house or sue to be paid. In the City of Myrtle Beach, electrical, plumbing, gas and mechanical work each need a trade permit.

### Houses built before 1978
Many of the cheapest houses are old enough to have lead paint. In a house built before 1978, anyone paid to do work that disturbs paint must be certified in lead-safe work. The EPA says the rule applies to a flipper doing their own work too. Small patches are outside it: 6 square feet of paint or less in a room, or 20 square feet or less outside. Replacing windows is always covered.

### Houses in a flood zone
This is the rule that can end a flip. If the work costs 50 percent or more of the building's value before the work, not counting the land, the federal flood program calls it a substantial improvement. Work to fix code violations an inspector has cited, and some work on historic buildings, are left out of that count.
In unincorporated Horry County , the whole house must then meet the rules for a new building. In a high-risk flood zone marked AE on the flood map, that means a lowest floor at least 3 feet above the flood height shown on the flood map for that spot.
In the City of Myrtle Beach , work on a building in a flood zone that does not meet today's flood rules must cost less than 50 percent of the building's value.
For an older house low to the ground, the rule can mean raising it or keeping the job under the limit. We check the flood zone and the county's building value before you offer, so you know the repair budget the rule allows. Our coastal insurance page covers flood insurance on the finished house.

## How does a finished flip sell here?
Most of our buyers for a finished flip are moving from out of state, or retiring. We spend several thousand dollars a month advertising to buyers moving to the Grand Strand, so a finished flip goes in front of them the day it lists. Lighter repairs sometimes suit the rental buyers on our list before the house reaches the open market.
One investor here inherited a house and had it fully repaired over about two and a half months. An agent at Chapter3 advertised it for sale while the work was going on. It went under contract a week before the work finished, and it closed for cash the day construction ended. Repaired, the house was worth about $390,000.
Advertise before the work ends. The loan, the tax and the insurance stop the day the house sells.
Plan to list by March. The fewest homes sell here in January and February. Every other month, about 800 to 1,050 sell, and prices move little, so the season gives you more buyers, not a higher price.

## What do you owe when you sell?
When you sell a house as an investor, you give the buyer South Carolina's property condition disclosure , the same form any owner gives. There is no exemption for investors, and it goes to the buyer before both sides sign.
When you sell most homes built before 1978, you also give the buyer the EPA's lead pamphlet and a lead disclosure, and the buyer gets 10 days to have the paint tested unless the buyer waives it. If the buyer asks for a termite letter, only a licensed pest control company may issue it.
A gain on a house held one year or less is a short-term gain , taxed as ordinary income. If you flip as a business, a house held mainly for sale to customers is not a capital asset, so its gain is not a capital gain at all. A flip also cannot go into a 1031 exchange .
South Carolina's 44 percent deduction on capital gains is for property held more than a year, so a flip gets none of it. For 2026, South Carolina's top rate is 5.21 percent on income above $30,000. Talk to a tax advisor before your first sale.

## Is wholesaling allowed in South Carolina?
Not the way it used to work. South Carolina's 2024 license law defines wholesaling as holding a contract to buy a home and then marketing the house to another buyer before you own it. Marketing someone else's property for pay is a broker's work and needs a license. A real estate brokerage and its agents may not wholesale or help a wholesaler. Assigning the contract itself is not wholesaling under the law.
The agents at Chapter3 have sold on the Grand Strand for decades and often hear about discounted houses, such as estate sales and new foreclosures, before they reach the big listing websites.

## How do you pay for a flip?
Many flips use a hard money loan, a short-term loan that closes quickly and can pay for part of the repairs. Its rate is higher than a normal mortgage, so every extra month you own the house costs you money. Our preferred lender, BrickWood Mortgage , offers fix-and-flip and bridge loans, so the purchase, the loan and the repair budget are planned together.

Cash is stronger. Bank-owned and off-market houses usually go to the buyer who can close soonest, and cash has no appraisal to fail. It also removes the largest holding cost, the loan interest.
You can still win with a loan off-market, where there is no cash offer to lose to. Our agents talk to owners before a house is listed and learn what the seller needs. Then we build the offer around it: the closing date, a shorter inspection, more earnest money, or a price that pays the seller for waiting on your loan.
Keep a backup plan. We run each address through our rental analyzer too, so you know what it would rent for if it does not sell. If it would rent well, you can refinance into a DSCR loan , which is approved on the rent instead of your tax returns, and keep it. That is the BRRRR strategy : buy, fix, rent, refinance, repeat.

Common questions

## Fix and flip FAQ

### How long does a flip take in Myrtle Beach?
About six months from purchase to resale. The middle home resold within a year in Horry County sold again 191 days after its purchase, and the middle half took about four to ten months.

### Can I flip a house in Myrtle Beach from out of state?
Yes. A Chapter3 agent walks the house on video, runs the numbers, and lines up the closing attorney and the inspector. Our page for out-of-state buyers explains how a closing works from a distance.

### Do I have to use BrickWood Mortgage?
No. You may use any lender you like. BrickWood Mortgage is our preferred lender for fix-and-flip and bridge loans.

### Do you need a license to flip houses in South Carolina?
No real estate license is needed to buy and sell a house you own. The contractors you hire need theirs, and the permits section above shows which work needs a license.

## 1031 Exchange in South Carolina | Chapter3 Realty

Summary: Delayed and reverse 1031 exchanges in South Carolina: deadlines, financing, withholding, and how we find replacement property in Myrtle Beach.

Tax strategy

# 1031 exchange in South Carolina.
By Devin Day , Operations Officer · Reviewed by Tim Nash , Broker-in-Charge · Updated November 1, 2026
A 1031 exchange lets you sell one South Carolina rental, buy another, and put off the tax bill. The 45 and 180 day deadlines, and the identification rules, explained.
Talk through your exchange

The basics

## What a 1031 exchange is

A 1031 exchange means you sell one rental, buy another, and put off the tax bill on your profit. The tax is delayed, not erased, and the deadlines are strict. Call us before you list, and we line up the sale, the next property, and the loan. That sequence is routine for our agents here, because 1031 buyers are one of the largest groups of investors Chapter3 works with on the Grand Strand.

The paperwork uses fancy names for plain things. The relinquished property is just the property you sell. The replacement property is the property you buy. A qualified intermediary, a neutral company that holds your money between the two sales, stands in the middle. You never touch the cash. The boxes below sum up the trade.

Why people do it

- + Put off the whole tax bill

- + Trade up into a bigger property

- + Keep all your money invested

What can go wrong

- ! Miss day 45 or day 180 and the tax is due

- ! Touch the money yourself and the deal is dead

- ! Rushed picks make bad buys

1031 replacement buyers are one of the largest groups of investors we work with. The usual shape: sell in an expensive market, buy on the Grand Strand, where the same money buys more property and the rents hold up.

One client, based in New York and buying with Tim for years, owns more than 200 rental properties, most of them condo units here. When a property has used up its depreciation, he sells it and trades the money up into a larger property through a 1031 exchange. The bigger purchase adds new depreciable value on top of what carried over, and the tax on the sale stays deferred. Residential rental buildings depreciate over 27.5 years, so a long-held rental eventually stops sheltering its own income. That is the point where many investors exchange instead of hold. How depreciation recapture builds up, and what a study does to the size of it, is on our cost segregation page .

The deadlines

## The exchange step by step, and what we do at each one

Both clocks start the day your sale closes, and they run at the same time. Day 45 to name the next property, day 180 to own it. The work happens in this order.

- 1 Before you list. Pick a qualified intermediary, the neutral company that will hold your money, and tell your closing attorney an exchange is coming. Our agents start the replacement search now rather than after the sale, because the 45 days are the tight part.

- 2 Your sale closes. The clock starts. The money goes straight to the intermediary. Touch it yourself and the exchange is over. We work the closing with your attorney to keep that clean.

- 3 Days 1 to 45. Shop with the numbers. Your replacement is an investment, so we judge candidates on rent, cap rate and tenant history, not on the finishes. We search the Coastal Carolinas MLS and bring you a short list, usually two or three strong picks and a backup.

- 4 Day 45. Name what you might buy, in writing. The list has to be signed by you and delivered to the intermediary. Telling your own agent, attorney or accountant does not count. We draft the list with you and send it in time.

- 5 The loan runs alongside all of this. Most exchanges need financing, and that loan has to close inside the same 180 days. We bring the lender in during the search so the two move together.

- 6 Day 180. You close, and the tax stays deferred. The purchase has to be finished by then. Our closing attorney, your intermediary and the lender all work to the same date, and we handle the South Carolina withholding paperwork covered further down.

How the day 45 list works. You choose one of three ways to write it. Name up to three properties at any price, which is what nearly everyone does. Name more than three, as long as the whole list adds up to no more than twice what you sold for. Or name as many as you like, if you end up buying at least 95 percent of what you listed. The practical job is to have three properties you would be happy to own by day 45, and bringing you those three is our part.

Two things that end exchanges. The window can be shorter than 180 days, because the exchange must be finished by the due date of your tax return for the year of the sale, extensions included. A late-year seller may need to file a tax extension to keep the full window. The dates themselves never move. The IRS extends them only for presidentially declared disasters.

Our closing attorneys, insurers and lending partner have all worked to these two dates with Chapter3 before. An exchange that is a scramble for a brokerage doing its first one is routine for our team on the Grand Strand. Run candidates through the long-term rental analyzer while you shop, so day 45 names a property you already trust.
Start your exchange plan Call 854.333.2135

Financing

## The replacement loan must close inside the 180 days too

To put off the whole tax bill, the property you buy usually has to cost as much or more. Most exchanges need a loan for that, and the loan must close inside the 180 days. We can bring a lender in early, so the search and the loan move together.

Many exchange buyers use a DSCR loan , where the loan qualifies on the property's rent, not your tax returns. A 1031 is a tax move, so confirm your plan with a qualified intermediary and a tax advisor.

The standard kind

## The delayed 1031 exchange
When investors say 1031 exchange, they almost always mean a delayed exchange. You close the sale first, the qualified intermediary takes the money, and then you buy the replacement inside the two windows: 45 days to name it, 180 days to close it. Everything on this page applies to that structure.
Our broker-in-charge, Tim Nash, has sold on the Grand Strand for more than 30 years and has worked 1031 exchanges for investors here, and his advice is always the same: build the replacement shortlist before the sale closes. The 45 days move faster than anyone expects, and the exchanges that get in trouble are usually the ones that started shopping on day one instead of a month before listing.

Buying first

## The reverse 1031 exchange
A reverse exchange flips the order: you buy the replacement first, then sell the old property within 180 days. The rules do not let you hold title to both at once, so a company created by your qualified intermediary, called an exchange accommodation titleholder, parks the title on one property while your sale closes.
Reverse exchanges cost more in intermediary fees, and financing is harder because the loan closes while title sits with the parking company. Fewer lenders will do that, and the ones that will want more lead time. A reverse makes sense when the right property shows up before your sale is ready. If that is your situation, call your intermediary and us earlier than feels necessary. If you want the deferral without managing anything again, the hands-off alternative is a DST .

South Carolina detail

## Selling from out of state: South Carolina withholding
When a nonresident sells South Carolina real estate, the state normally keeps back part of the money at closing. It is called nonresident withholding. In a properly structured 1031 exchange, the seller completes a state affidavit so the withholding matches the tax due, which on a fully deferred exchange is often nothing. The current withholding rate, forms, and refund mechanics are on our capital gains page .
The closing attorney and your qualified intermediary prepare that form as part of the closing. The exact rules and percentages change, so Chapter3 confirms the current requirement with the closing attorney on every exchange we handle here. The official source is the South Carolina Department of Revenue .

Common questions

## Frequently asked questions

### Does a 1031 exchange work in South Carolina?
Yes. South Carolina follows the federal 1031 rules, so an investor can defer capital gains tax by exchanging one investment property for another. The Grand Strand is a common replacement market for investors trading out of higher-priced areas.

### What are the 1031 exchange deadlines?
Two clocks start the day you close the sale: 45 days to identify replacement properties in writing, and 180 days to close on one. They run together, and missing either deadline makes the deferred gain taxable.

### Do I need financing for a 1031 exchange?
Usually. To fully defer the tax, the replacement property generally must be equal or greater in value with all proceeds reinvested, which typically requires a loan that closes inside the 180-day window. Because Chapter3 Realty and BrickWood Mortgage work closely together, the purchase and the loan move in step, which helps the replacement close inside the window.

### Can I do a 1031 exchange into multiple properties?
Yes. Many investors exchange one appreciated property into several Grand Strand rentals. The identification rules allow up to three properties of any value. You can name more than three only if their combined value stays within 200 percent of the sale, or any number if you close on at least 95 percent of the value identified. A qualified intermediary and a tax advisor should confirm the structure.

### Who holds the money during a 1031 exchange?
A qualified intermediary holds the sale proceeds between the two closings. You cannot take possession of the funds, or the exchange is disqualified. This is a tax matter, so professional guidance is essential.

### What is a delayed 1031 exchange?
It is the standard structure: you sell first, a qualified intermediary holds the proceeds, and you buy the replacement within the 45-day identification window and the 180-day closing window. When people say 1031 exchange, they usually mean a delayed exchange.

### How does a reverse 1031 exchange work?
You buy the replacement first, then sell the old property within 180 days. A company set up by your qualified intermediary holds title to one of the properties in the meantime. Reverse exchanges cost more, fewer lenders finance them, and they need more lead time.

### Can the 45-day or 180-day deadline be extended?
No, with one exception: the IRS extends 1031 deadlines only when it issues disaster relief for a presidentially declared disaster. Illness, financing delays, a failed inspection or a seller who backs out do not extend anything. There is a second cutoff too: the exchange must be complete by the due date of your tax return for the year of the sale, including extensions. A late-year seller may need to file a tax extension to keep the full 180 days.

### Can I do a 1031 exchange into South Carolina from another state?
Yes. The 1031 rules are federal, so you can sell in any state and buy your replacement on the Grand Strand. Plan for South Carolina nonresident withholding at closing; in a proper exchange the closing attorney files an affidavit so you are not over-withheld.

Sources: IRS, Like-Kind Exchanges Under IRC Section 1031 , IRS Form 8824 instructions , IRS Publication 527 on depreciation , South Carolina Department of Revenue . We are not tax advisers; confirm your exchange with a qualified intermediary and a tax professional.

# How do you rent a Myrtle Beach house to J-1 students? The program, the employers, the beds, the rules.
By Devin Day , Operations Officer · Reviewed by Tim Nash , Broker-in-Charge · Updated September 16, 2026
J-1 students staff the Myrtle Beach summer and rent by the bed. A house holds as many as its bedroom floor area allows, at $100 to $140 a week each.
Talk about buying a J-1 house

The short answer
J-1 students are college students from abroad, here on a four-month summer work visa. South Carolina hosted about 3,000 of them in 2025. Myrtle Beach was the fourth busiest destination in the country.
They rent by the bed, three or four to a room, at about $100 to $140 a week each. That is the appeal. One house, four months, several rents at once.
The limit is how many people the house may lawfully hold. The city counts bedroom floor area, 70 square feet for the first person and 50 for each one after that. A 2,500 square foot four-bedroom house holds about 10 to 13 people. A garage holds none.
We have walked through a house here with more than 60 J-1 students living in it. That is the case this page tells you not to copy, and the sections below say why.

## What is a J-1 student, and why do they rent in Myrtle Beach?
A J-1 student is a full-time college student from another country on a Summer Work Travel visa. The program allows up to four months of seasonal work during the student's summer break, and no extension. Most students have a job before they arrive , through a sponsor organization that screens them and vets the employer.
They rent here because the jobs are here. Myrtle Beach has about 35,000 residents and about 17 million visitors a year . Hotels, restaurants and attractions need summer staff the town cannot supply. The city has hosted about 8,500 J-1 students since 2018 .
The State Department counted 104,609 Summer Work Travel students in 2025 . South Carolina had 3,003 of them, the 14th most of any state. Myrtle Beach was the fourth busiest destination in the country , after Ocean City, Orlando and Wisconsin Dells. No source gives the exact Myrtle Beach count.
The top sending countries in 2025 were Jamaica, Thailand, Mexico, Peru, Romania, Turkey, Ecuador and the Dominican Republic. Each country has its own program window . Most run May to September. Peru, Argentina, Brazil, Chile and South Africa run December to April, so some students are here in winter.

## Which employers hire the most J-1 students, and do they house them?
The employers with the most seasonal jobs. The president of Lazarus Entertainment Group said in November 2024 that 150 of the 500 summer staff at Myrtle Waves Water Park and Broadway Grand Prix are J-1 students. He said he had been pre-renting houses around the city to get enough beds. He had reserved 150 of the 300 beds in the new residence hall for the next summer.
The owner of Extreme Pizza and Toasted Yolk Cafe told a reporter in February 2026 that without the students the summer would be like 2021. That was the year no one had enough staff. Sponsor job listings for the area show a pizza restaurant, a diner chain and an oceanfront resort offering housing at $100 a week. A beachwear chain offers it at $110 a week, taken from the paycheck.
The rule puts the housing duty on the sponsor, not the employer. If the employer does not provide housing, the sponsor must actively and immediately assist the student in finding it. The sponsor must also consider housing that meets local codes when it places the job. No rule requires a sponsor to inspect or approve a private landlord's house, and no rule caps the rent.
One purpose-built building exists. The International Residence Hall on Globe Drive has more than 300 beds, four to a room, with weekly rent. It opened in May 2025 , with tax incentives from the city. More buildings are planned; the reported totals differ by source. Its rent is not published.
How students find a house What the source says
Employer housing first Sponsors tell students they learn at hiring whether the employer offers housing
Their own search Sponsors list Craigslist, Apartments.com, Roommates.com, Zillow and Facebook groups
Houses that advertise to them Two North Myrtle Beach operators list rooms by the week on their own sites
A landlord who works with employers One North Myrtle Beach landlord has placed seasonal workers for employers for ten years
The city's orientation site Lists one provider, the residence hall, and warns about deposit scams

There is no sponsor portal where a landlord signs up. The visitor bureau held a J-1 forum for employers, landlords and sponsors in February 2026. Employers pre-rent, and students search. A house that an employer has rented for its staff, year after year, is the steadiest version of this rental.

## How much rent does a J-1 house collect in Myrtle Beach?
Rent is per bed, per week, with the kitchen, Wi-Fi and laundry included. One North Myrtle Beach operator lists $120 a week in spring and $130 in summer , three to a room, with a 90-day minimum lease and a $260 deposit. Another lists $130 and $140 a week , four to a room in bunk beds, with a $250 deposit. Employer housing in the sponsor listings is $100 to $110 a week.
That is about $430 to $610 a month per person. Our earlier figure of $500 to $700 a month came from our own observation. The listings are lower, so this page uses the listings.

One sponsor caps a student's rent at a third of gross pay . At 32 hours a week, the minimum in several local listings, a third of pay is a few hundred dollars a month. The rent per bed has a ceiling the students' wages put on it.

## How many people can a Myrtle Beach house lawfully hold?
Inside the City of Myrtle Beach the answer comes from bedroom floor area. The city adopts the International Property Maintenance Code . Its occupancy section says a bedroom for one person needs 70 square feet, and a bedroom for two or more needs 50 square feet for each person. Kitchens and nonhabitable spaces cannot be slept in. Every bedroom needs a path to a toilet without passing through another bedroom.
A 2,500 square foot four-bedroom house: one 14 by 16 foot bedroom holds four people. Three 12 by 12 foot bedrooms hold two each. That is ten people. If the three smaller bedrooms are 12 by 14 feet, they hold three each, and the house holds thirteen. A detached garage holds no one unless it was converted under a permit with a certificate of occupancy.
North Myrtle Beach and the unincorporated county do not list the property maintenance code among their adopted codes, as mirrored online. They enforce through the building codes, their unfit-dwelling rules and, in North Myrtle Beach, the zoning definitions. Confirm the count for the exact house with the building department before you model the rent. We do that with you.

## What happens if you put too many people in the house?
We have walked through a house here with more than 60 J-1 students living in it. Do not copy it.
The fines are per day. A code violation in the city is a civil fine of up to $200 . After seven days' notice to fix it, the fine is up to $2,000 for each day it continues. Every rental in the city needs a business license . Renting without one is a misdemeanor, with up to a $500 fine and 30 days, and each day is a separate offense.
Enforcement happens, and it starts with complaints. In July 2021 a homeowner was charged for housing three J-1 students in a garage apartment he built without permits; the students were moved. In 2025 the city described reports of more than ten students in a two-bedroom space . In 2026 the fire marshal described past citations for four or five students in one bed with an air mattress in the closet.

## Is the J-1 housing market already full?
No. The people who need the beds have said so in public, by name.
The owner of Lazarus Entertainment Group said securing beds that met his standards was hard . He described putting deposits on houses all over Myrtle Beach to get enough of them, and called it difficult and challenging. He hires about 150 J-1 students a season out of 500 seasonal staff.
The city manager said the same from the other side . When the city finds a house with too many people in it, it has to have somewhere to move those young adults to. The city needs spare beds to exist before it can enforce anything.
Then count it.

Even finished, the purpose-built building holds under half the students who work here. The rest need a house.
The gap is not only beds. It is clean beds. The mayor said in 2024 that some properties are not taken care of as they should be , and that students have been taken advantage of. A partner in the residence hall said he had heard of 19 people in one house . A house inside the lawful count, with a real bed for each person, is competing against that.

## How do you find J-1 students to rent to?
Start with the employers, not the students. The big ones rent houses before the season and put their own staff in them. The president of Lazarus Entertainment Group described putting deposits on houses all over Myrtle Beach to get enough beds, and called it difficult. A house an employer takes every year fills with no advertising at all.
Sponsors will not do it for you. The State Department lists every sponsor by name and you can call them. They no longer keep lists of landlords, and they have no staff for placing students in private houses. The rule says only that the sponsor must help the student find housing and must send information about available housing before the student leaves home. Nobody inspects or approves your house.
Where to look What it gets you

Who do you ask about that site? The police department runs it as the International Student Outreach Program , with the area chamber and the hospitality association. The program takes calls at 843-918-1806 and email at j1studentoutreach@cityofmyrtlebeach.com . The hospitality association is at 843-626-9668 . Be straight about what you are asking. Neither publishes a landlord list, so you are asking them to point students at a house, not to add you to a form.
Write the listing the way a student reads it. The weekly rent per bed. The deposit and what comes back. How far to work, in miles. A photo of the bed. Sponsors tell students to ask those exact questions , so answer them before they ask.
List the house over the winter. Employers plan the season months ahead, and the students land in May. A house first listed in March is late.

## What do J-1 students look for in a Myrtle Beach rental?

- Close to work without a car. One operator says all its houses are under two miles from the job and most students rent or buy a bike. Every Coast RTA bus carries two bikes . A house near the oceanfront employers or on a bus route fills first.

- A kitchen, Wi-Fi and laundry. Every local listing advertises all three. Linens are sometimes included.

- Weekly rent and a clear deposit. Sponsors tell students to ask the weekly cost, the deposit and what is refundable , and to check the occupancy limit in the lease.

- No scams. The city's orientation site warns students about people who take deposits and provide no room . Sponsors tell them never to wire money before arrival. A landlord who shows the house on a video call and takes the deposit on arrival removes that fear.

- Smoke detectors. Sponsors tell students to check for them. The 2013 motel closure in the city was for missing detectors and seven or eight people in rooms built for four.

## How do you screen and lease to J-1 tenants?
One lease per person, in English. Sponsors assume an English lease and tell students to read it and keep a signed copy. Put the move-in and move-out dates, the rent, the deposit and the occupancy limit in it. The student must report the address to the sponsor within ten days , so the sponsor has your address on file.
Screen every applicant the same way. National origin is a protected class , and a rule that all tenants must speak English is a practice federal housing regulators call suspect . A passport is a photo ID. Sponsors tell students a landlord can ask for photo ID, an employer letter and proof of funds from home. Every student has the sponsor's 24-hour number and can give it to you.
End the lease before the program does. The visa allows four months plus 30 days to travel, and the student must leave the country by then. A fixed term that ends on the job's end date, with the deposit returned to an address abroad, is the clean version. The landlord rules page has the deposit clock and the notices.

## What happens if you need to evict a J-1 tenant?
The same law as any tenant. The state landlord and tenant act applies to every dwelling in the state and says nothing about citizenship. The grounds are unpaid rent, a term that has ended, or a broken lease . More people in the house than the lease allows is a broken lease, and the fourteen-day notice applies.
Weekly rent with no fixed term makes a week-to-week tenancy, which either side ends on seven days' written notice. A fixed term ends on its date. Fifteen days of unexplained absence after unpaid rent is abandonment . The magistrate process, the writ and the fees are on the landlord rules page .
The student's program does not end with the housing. Losing housing is not a ground for termination . The sponsor must actively and immediately help the student find new housing , and the student reports the new address within ten days. Sponsors list eviction as a reason to call their 24-hour line. In the 2021 garage case the city moved the students the same day.
The cost of an eviction on a four-month lease is the season. A house that stays inside the lawful count, with one lease per person and the sponsor's number in the file, rarely needs one. In Chapter3's files, the problem houses are the overfilled ones, not the tenants.

## What do you do with the house the other eight months?
The season is four months because the visa allows four . A house that sits empty from October is a worse rental than a house on one yearly lease. Plan the other eight months before you buy, not after.
Some students are here in winter. Peru, Argentina, Brazil, Chile and South Africa run December to April , so their students work our winter. How many reach this area is not published.
The residence hall has said what it does. A partner in it said H-2B workers stay nine months a year , so it expects lower winter occupancy rather than an empty building. H-2B is the other seasonal visa. Those workers staff the same hotels, golf courses and restaurants, and they stay longer than a J-1 student can.

Run the comparison before you buy. Four months by the bed, from the table above, collects about what a yearly lease on the same house collects in twelve. You beat a yearly lease only if you fill those eight months.
Wear is the part people forget. Ten people use a house harder than three. Budget paint and cleaning every autumn. Put the turnover between tenants into the year you model.

## What can go wrong with a J-1 rental?
Neighbors notice a full house, and the city says neighbors are how it learns about overcrowding. Stay inside the lawful count and that call does not come.
The residence hall competes at the low end, three hundred beds at a time, with employers reserving blocks. A clean house inside the lawful count, near the jobs, competes on quality. A duplex or fourplex spreads the same model across units; the small multifamily page has the financing. Student rentals near the university are the year-round version.

# How to buy a duplex or fourplex in Myrtle Beach.
By Devin Day , Operations Officer · Chapter3 Realty · Updated October 27, 2026
Two, three or four rent checks from one Myrtle Beach building, financed like a regular home: how to buy a duplex, triplex or fourplex here, and who rents the units.
Talk through a building

The five steps

## How small multifamily works, step by step

- 1 Find a building of two to four units. Four units or fewer keeps it on a regular home loan.

- 2 Add up the rent roll. That is the combined rent from every unit, not the best one.

- 3 Weigh it against the whole building&#x27;s costs. Payment, taxes, insurance and maintenance for all units together.

- 4 Decide whether you will live in one. Living in a unit opens owner-occupied loans with far less money down.

- 5 Budget for more tenants. More units means more calls, and one roof or HVAC bill hits every unit at once.

Small multifamily means a duplex, triplex, or fourplex. That is two, three, or four homes in one purchase, one loan, one roof. On the Grand Strand, these buildings cluster in Conway, the older parts of Myrtle Beach, and pockets of North Myrtle Beach. Chapter3 has sold in all three Grand Strand pockets and knows which blocks rent to year-round workers and which fill with summer staff. The boxes below give the ten-second version of the trade.
How scarce they are: the whole Grand Strand MLS usually shows fewer than one hundred multifamily listings of any size at a time, starting near $225,000 for a small duplex and running past $13 million for hotel-scale property. The two-to-four-unit slice of that is smaller still. That is why the good ones go under contract fast. It is also why Chapter3 watches the Grand Strand MLS for them daily and hears about some before they list, from the agents and property managers our team has worked with here for decades.
Who rents the units: year-round workers, and in summer the J-1 exchange students who staff the beach. J-1 groups rent by the person and fill a unit completely; the demand, the rates and the rules are on our J-1 rental guide .

Why people do it

- + Several rents from one purchase

- + One vacancy does not zero your income

- + Live in one unit, let the others pay the loan

What can go wrong

- ! More tenants means more calls

- ! One roof or HVAC bill hits every unit at once

- ! Good buildings are scarce and go fast

The four-unit line

## Four units or fewer keeps the loan simple

Lenders draw a hard line at four units. That line decides the kind of loan you can get and the cash you need.

2 to 4 units

- Counts as a regular home loan.

- Small down payment if you live there.

- Familiar paperwork and simpler rules.

5 or more units

- Counts as a commercial loan.

- Bigger down payment.

- Tougher rules and a tighter review.

Live in one, rent the rest

## House hacking, the low-cash way in

House hacking means you buy the building as your own home. You live in one unit and rent out the others. Their rent helps pay your loan. Tim has owned rentals in Horry County himself for years, and the building math on this page is the math he runs on his own.

Because you live there, you can use an owner-occupied loan like FHA on a two-to-four-unit building: a far smaller down payment than an investor loan, and a lower rate. Lenders generally expect you to live there about a year. After that, you can move out, rent your old unit, and keep the whole building.

Planning the live-in route? Start with our buyer guides for low-down-payment loans, including VA options. Buying purely as an investor? Look at a DSCR loan . DSCR means the loan qualifies on the property's rent, not your tax returns.

Check the math

## Judge the whole building, not one unit

A small multifamily deal succeeds or fails on its rent roll, the combined rent from every unit. Add up every rent. Then set that total against the loan payment, taxes, insurance, and repairs for the whole building.

Our long-term rental analyzer prices one unit at a time. Run each unit, add them up, and you can see the building's true picture. It is the same tool our agents use on every Grand Strand building we show, so the rent figures come from local leases rather than a national estimate. Want to compare other paths first? ## Frequently asked questions

### Is a duplex a good investment in Myrtle Beach?
Often, yes. A duplex gives you two rent checks from one purchase and one roof. It can be financed with a regular home loan. On the Grand Strand, duplexes cluster in Conway, older Myrtle Beach neighborhoods, and parts of North Myrtle Beach.

### What is the difference between a fourplex and a five-unit building?
Financing. A building with two to four units counts as residential, so regular home loans apply. At five units and up, the building counts as commercial. That means a commercial loan, a bigger down payment, and tougher rules.

### Can I live in one unit and rent the others?
Yes. That is house hacking. Buy a two-to-four-unit building as your home and you can use a low-down-payment loan such as FHA, conventional, or VA. The other units help cover the mortgage. Lenders generally expect you to live there about a year.

### How much down payment does a multifamily property need?
It depends on whether you live there. An owner-occupied duplex through fourplex can require a small down payment with the right loan. For a pure investment purchase, a DSCR loan needs a substantial down payment. DSCR means the loan qualifies on the property's rent, not your tax returns.

### How do I run the numbers on a triplex or fourplex?
Running the numbers just means checking the math the way a lender would. Start with the rent roll, the combined rent from every unit. Weigh it against the payment, taxes, insurance, and maintenance for the whole building. Our long-term rental analyzer gives you the per-unit numbers to build the total.

## A Myrtle Beach Condo in Litigation Can Be the Best Deal
URL: https://chapter3realty.com/buyers/condo-in-litigation/
Summary: Told no on a Myrtle Beach condo in litigation? When you can still buy, why lenders decline, and how one buyer got a steep oceanfront discount.

Home / Buyers / Condo in Litigation

A Real Grand Strand Deal

# A condo in litigation can be the best deal in Myrtle Beach.

By Devin Day , Operations Officer · Chapter3 Realty · Updated October 27, 2026

Conventional, FHA and VA loans all decline a condo building in litigation. The unit can still be bought, sometimes at a steep discount: one Grand Strand example, start to finish.

The short answer

## Yes, you can often buy it, and it can be the best deal available

A buyer in the area was set on a specific oceanfront unit. They loved it and were ready to put down more than a thousand dollars in earnest money to lock it up. Before that happened, a building study was run on the building. Better to spend the time up front than to watch a buyer wire earnest money and then fight to claw it back when something surfaces later.

What surfaced this time was significant: the building was in structural-defect litigation . For most buyers, that is where the deal ends. But the reading carried on, and the details told a different story.

Why lenders say no

## Active litigation fails the warrantability standard

A condo project in active litigation fails the warrantability standard that Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac, FHA, and VA all require, because lenders fear a large special assessment, or in the worst case a condemned building, landing on their collateral. Conventional, FHA, and VA financing all decline. By the lender rules, the unit was unfinanceable.

Why we kept reading

## A like-new building and sellers who could not sell is an opportunity

This pattern is common with aging condo buildings. As a building gets older, ordinary wear can reveal construction defects that were hidden when it was new. An association has only a limited legal window to bring a claim, so defect lawsuits tend to cluster as a building matures.

In this case, the association had already sued , the building had already repaired everything the suit was about , and the work left it in close to new condition. Meanwhile, the sellers inside the building were stuck, unable to find buyers while the litigation cloud hung over the project, and several were motivated to move.

The play

## So instead of walking away, our agent built a plan

The buyer went under contract, the mortgage underwriter was kept informed of exactly what was happening and why, and closing was set to wait until the litigation resolved. The week the building came out of litigation, it closed. It became one of the agent’s best sales.

The buyer got a steep discount on a building that was, by then, as good as new, on a unit they could not have financed a week earlier.

What it means for you

## The difference a building study makes

A public listing will not tell you that a project is in litigation, why it got there, whether the defects have been fixed, or whether the timing can work for you. Your agent should. When you work with a Chapter3 agent, we tell you everything we find about a building before you risk a dollar, and sometimes the thing that looks like a reason to run is the reason you get the deal.

Talk to a licensed agent

This is one buyer’s outcome, shared for illustration, not a promise of results or lending, tax, or legal advice. Condo warrantability and litigation situations vary; confirm your specific financing with a licensed lender.

Common Questions

## Frequently asked questions

### Can you get a mortgage on a condo in active litigation?
Usually not with conventional, FHA, or VA financing, because active litigation fails the warrantability standard, the condo-project rules those loans require. But the deal is not always dead: if the litigation is close to resolving, you can sometimes structure the contract to close once it clears, or use a non-warrantable / portfolio loan.

### Why do lenders decline condos in litigation?
Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac, FHA, and VA worry that a lawsuit could end in a large special assessment, or in the worst case a condemned building, that would damage the value of the collateral. They decline the whole project until the litigation resolves.

### Does a condo in litigation always mean you should walk away?
No. The details matter: what the suit is about, whether the repairs are already done, and how close it is to resolving. A building that has already fixed the defects and is near the end of its litigation can be a rare discount on a like-new project that most buyers cannot touch yet.

### What does it mean when a condo is non-warrantable?
A condo project that fails the project rules behind normal conventional and government loans, often because of litigation, a high investor-ownership ratio, or commercial space. These need a non-warrantable or portfolio loan, which is exactly the kind of financing our preferred lender can walk you through.

## Has This House Flooded? Myrtle Beach Flood History | Chapter3

Flood history

# Did this Myrtle Beach house flood before? How to find its flood history.

- About 3 in 4 resale houses for sale: the seller's form does not ask about Florence

- 45% of paid Florence claims were insured outside FEMA's zone

By Devin Day , Operations Officer · Reviewed by Tim Nash , Broker-in-Charge · Updated November 1, 2026
Five checks show it: FEMA's claim records, two flood maps, the county's records, repair permits and the house itself. You get all five for any house you send.

The short answer
FEMA's flood claim records go only to the owner, so we ask the seller for them. We put the house on FEMA's flood map and the county's map of Florence's flooding. We ask the county's staff about past floods and look for permits behind repairs. At the showing, we look for clues at the house and on its street.
We run these checks before you offer. If you learn of a flood after you sign, the South Carolina REALTORS sales contract gives you a due diligence period to end it.

Have us check a house's flood history
Send us the address

## How do you find out if a house has flooded before?
Our agents check five things. Each card says what that check can miss.

- Ask the seller for the claim records From the seller The Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) runs federal flood insurance. It will not give a buyer a house's flood insurance claims: federal privacy law bars it without the owner's consent.
We ask the seller for those, and for the insurance industry's claims report on the house , called CLUE.
What it misses: A flood on a house that had no flood insurance.

- Put the house on two flood maps Public maps: we pull them FEMA's flood map is a forecast of risk. After Florence, Horry County mapped how far Florence's water went .
We put the house on both maps. Our map of the two shows where they differ.
What it misses: Whether water got inside. The county's map shows the ground Florence's water covered, in that one storm.

- Ask the county's floodplain staff We ask the county Horry County's floodplain staff answer "Has my property ever flooded?" and keep the county's flood history, including where floods have repeated. The county also posts the signed surveys it has on file that show how high a floor is.
What it misses: A house inside a city. Each city keeps its own records, and we ask that city.

- Look for a permit behind every repair We ask the county or city Outside city limits in Horry County, any work on a building over $500 needs a permit. Inside a city, the city issues it. A flood repair done legally leaves a permit record .
What it misses: Work done with no permit. A repair with no record is a question we put to the seller.

- Read the house and the street At the showing We use the county's questions about water around a house . We look at whether water flows away from the house or stands next to the walls, whether the ditch or storm drain is clear, and whether the downspouts carry water well away.
On the street, a house raised above its older neighbors can be one that flooded and was rebuilt. Empty lots between houses can be a flood buyout.
What it misses: Proof. These are clues, and the records above confirm or rule them out.

### What if the seller will not send the records?
If the seller refuses, or does not answer, we tell you right away. You decide with what the maps, the county and the house showed: offer, offer less, or walk away.

### Can I back out if I find a flood after I sign?
Yes, inside the due diligence period on the South Carolina REALTORS sales contract. In that period the buyer can end the contract with a written notice of termination to the seller. We tell you what ending it would cost under the contract you sign, before you sign it. That is why we run these checks first.

## Does a seller have to disclose flooding in South Carolina?
Yes, on the state's disclosure form, but only for the years the seller owned the house. South Carolina law requires the form for a home with one to four units. The seller hands it over before you sign the contract, unless the contract says otherwise.
The form asks about floods, flood insurance claims, flood repairs and federal flood aid, each only for the seller's years. One question asks about any flood risk the seller knows of.
For about 3 in 4 resale houses for sale here, Florence came before the seller bought Before the seller bought The form does not ask.

Resale houses for sale (not new builds) that we could match to a county parcel. Our count, from Horry County's parcel records and homes for sale counted in aggregate.

### What does "No Representation" mean?
It is an answer on the form. A seller may choose it only when they do not have the knowledge to answer. The form says a seller may not choose it to avoid a question, must still disclose what they know, and is not freed from liability by it.

### Which sales need no disclosure form?
Some sales need no form at all. Among them are estate and trust sales, foreclosure sales, public auctions, the first sale of a new home no one has lived in , and a sale where both sides agree in writing to skip it. In those sales, the five checks matter more.

## Can a house flood if it is not in a flood zone?
Yes, and in Horry County it happens most in rain and river floods. Since 1978, nearly 1 in 4 paid flood insurance claims here were on buildings insured as outside FEMA's high-risk zone. That means the policy was priced for a lower-risk zone.

In storm surge, almost every paid claim here was inside FEMA's high-risk zone. In rain and river floods, far more were outside it.

### What Florence did
During Hurricane Florence in 2018, the Waccamaw River at Conway rose to a record crest , more than three feet above the old record from Hurricane Matthew in 2016 . Nearly 1,000 homes and businesses near the river flooded, many of them badly.

### Does a clean claim history mean the house never flooded?
No. A house with no flood insurance leaves no flood claim. Horry County has about one federal flood policy for every seven residential buildings, so most houses here have no federal flood policy to claim on.

## Should you buy a house that flooded?
Buy a house that flooded only when three things are true. Our agents check each one.

- It was repaired with permits Each flood repair has its permit on file, as in check 4.
We match each repair to its permit record.

- It is raised, or its risk is known If repairs after a flood cost 50 percent or more of the house's value before it, the house must be raised above the flood height on FEMA's map .
We pull the survey of how high its floor sits.

- You know the flood insurance cost A house's federal flood claims stay with the address , not the owner, and its claim history can raise the cost of its flood insurance.
We help you get a flood insurance quote on the house.

A house outside the high-risk zone can still be a repeat-flood house: nearly 1 in 5 Horry County properties on FEMA's list of repeat flood claims are outside it. The worst, which FEMA calls severe repetitive loss , pay at least 15 percent more for federal flood insurance.
A seller who took federal flood aid that required flood insurance must tell you in writing, in the sale papers, that you must keep flood insurance on the house. Federal law requires it.

### Why does a street have empty lots between houses?
Sometimes because of a flood buyout. The state's voluntary buyout program has bought dozens of homes in the Socastee area that flooded again and again. It tears the houses down, and the land stays open green space.
When a house you like sits beside empty lots, we ask the county's floodplain staff about the street's flood history.

## What if the seller did not disclose flooding?
A seller who knowingly gives false, incomplete or misleading answers on the form is liable for the buyer's actual damages from them, and court costs. The court may also award reasonable attorney fees to whichever side wins.
Your own buyer's agent , under a written agreement, must tell you every serious problem the agent knows of. A fact that significantly lowers the value or the soundness of the house counts.
Where a complaint about a flood no one told you about goes The problem Who handles it
A seller who knew and did not tell you A South Carolina real estate attorney
An agent who knew and did not tell you Real Estate Commission and an attorney
A dispute over the sales contract An attorney, not the Commission

The Real Estate Commission takes complaints against licensed agents, not private sellers, and it does not handle contract disputes. Claims like these have deadlines in South Carolina law . Many are three years, and for fraud the time starts when the fraud is discovered.
If you already bought a house that flooded and the seller hid it, talk to a South Carolina real estate attorney. We work with several attorneys here and can introduce you. Chapter3 Realty does not give legal advice.

### How a flood check can change an offer
Example: A buyer likes a house near the Waccamaw River. The seller bought after Florence and answers No to every flood question on the form.
A Chapter3 agent puts the lot on the county's Florence flood map. Florence's water covered the yard. The agent asks for the house's FEMA claim records, and the seller will not send them.
The buyer walks away and offers on a house a mile off, on land the water did not cover.

The form never asked about that flood. The county's map showed it.

Common questions

## Flood history questions

### Can I get a CLUE report on a house I want to buy?
No. Only the owner, an insurer or a lender can order the CLUE report on a house, and it covers only recent years. We ask the seller to order it.

### Can I see FEMA flood claims by address?
Not until you own the house. Once you do, you can ask FEMA for its claims, including those from before you owned it.

### What is a severe repetitive loss property?
Severe repetitive loss is FEMA's label for a house that has flooded again and again. FEMA uses it for four or more paid flood claims over $5,000 each, or for building payments that add up to more than the house is worth, with two of them within 10 years of each other. The label stays with the address when the house sells.

### Will the lender tell me if the house is in a flood zone?
Yes, if the house is in FEMA's high-risk zone and the loan is from a bank or other federally regulated lender. The lender must make sure you are told in writing a reasonable time before you sign. The notice is about the zone, not about past floods.

## Myrtle Beach DST 1031 Exchange: Fees, Limits, Exits | Chapter3
URL: https://chapter3realty.com/invest/strategies/dst/
Summary: A DST (Delaware statutory trust) lets you sell a rental, put off the tax and stop managing. What it costs, who can buy one and what you give up.

Home / Invest / DST
Strategy

# DST: the hands-off 1031 for a Grand Strand rental Swap a Grand Strand rental for a share of a large property: no tenants, tax put off, about 6% to sales commissions.

- What you get No tenants, tax later

- Who can buy $1M+ net worth or $200K+ income

- Usual minimum $100,000

- Sales commission About 6% of your money

By Devin Day , Operations Officer · Reviewed by Tim Nash , Broker-in-Charge · Updated November 1, 2026
A Delaware statutory trust (DST) owns real estate and sells shares in it. A share can replace your rental in a 1031 exchange.

The short answer
In a DST, a sponsor, the real estate company that forms the trust, buys the property and runs it. You get a share of the cash it has left over. In return, you usually get your money back only when the trust sells, the payout can fall, and sales commissions come out of your money first.
It fits only if you are done managing, pass the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) wealth test, and will not need the money for years.

We time the sale of your Grand Strand rental to your exchange deadlines.
