- Three choices

- How a DST works

- What you give up

- Who can buy

- Cost and minimum

- Getting out

- As a 1031 backup

- DSTs here

- What we do

- DST questions

## Should you sell your Grand Strand rental into a DST, another rental, or pay the tax?
On a $400,000 rental sale on the Grand Strand, the Myrtle Beach area, you choose between paying the tax now, keeping the work of a rental, or giving up control of the money. The numbers are our example, worked through below.
Three choices for our $400,000 example sale What changes Sell and pay the tax 1031 into another rental 1031 into a DST
Tax this year about $39,000, or more at higher incomes None yet None yet
Income None from this rental The rent, less your costs A share of leftover cash, not fixed
Work each month None Yours, or a manager's None
When you get the money At closing When you sell that rental When the trust sells

### Which one fits

- A DST, if you would rather own a share of a large property someone else runs than a rental of your own.

- Another rental here, if you want to pick the property, set the rent and decide when to sell. Our 1031 exchange guide covers the deadlines and how we find a replacement on the Grand Strand.

- Paying the tax, if you want the cash now, or the tax is small next to what a DST would cost you to enter.

- Keeping the rental, if the work is the only problem. A property manager takes the calls, and our page on how long to hold a rental shows what waiting has meant here.

## Why does the IRS allow a DST in a 1031 exchange, and who sells one?
The IRS, in Revenue Ruling 2004-86 , has ruled that you may trade a rental for a share of a Delaware statutory trust with no tax on the gain yet. The trust must follow the ruling's limits, and the other 1031 rules must be met.
You buy the share through a securities firm or broker, called the DST broker on this page. Anyone who sells you a DST share must be registered with the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority (FINRA), the SEC or the state before they can sell you anything. FINRA's BrokerCheck lists each securities firm and broker, with their licenses and record.

## What do you give up in a DST, and can you lose money?
The ruling requires these limits on the trust:

- The trust cannot take in new money from anyone. A large repair has to be paid from the trust's own cash. That cash is not paid out to you.

- It cannot refinance its loan or sign a new lease. In the ruling, the trust may sign a new lease only if its tenant goes bankrupt or insolvent. A DST with many tenants, such as an apartment community, can lease the whole property to one master tenant. In one large sponsor's program , the master tenant is a company the sponsor owns. It signs the tenants, pays the costs of running the property and pays the trust its rent. Either way, the trust depends on one tenant's rent.

- You have no say in when the property sells. The trust's manager decides.

### What does a DST pay you?
The trust pays out the cash the property has left, less reserves, on a set schedule. In the IRS ruling, that is every quarter. The amount moves with the rent and with the cash held back for repairs.
The SEC filings we checked have no payout figure. If the sponsor projects a payout, the projection is in its offering document, often called a private placement memorandum (PPM).
To compare a DST with your rental, set the PPM's projected payout for a year on your share next to what your rental leaves you in a year: the rent, less every cost you pay, the mortgage included. Ask the DST broker for the PPM before you name a DST in your exchange, and look for four things in it:

- Every fee, with its amount.

- The projected payout, and what it rests on.

- How long the sponsor plans to hold the property.

- Who the tenants are, and how long their leases run.

### Can you get back less than you put in?
Yes. You get back your share of what is left of the sale price after the trust's loan is paid off. The sales commissions and the sponsor's fees were paid out of the money first, so the property has to gain value before your share is worth what you paid. If it sells for less than the trust paid, you get back less still.

## Who can buy a DST?
Most DSTs are sold only to buyers who pass the SEC's wealth test, called accredited investors . For a person, you pass with either of these:

### Net worth
Over $1 million Alone or with a spouse or partner, not counting your home.

### Income
Over $200,000 Or $300,000 with a spouse or partner, in each of the last two years, with the same expected this year.

Holders of certain securities licenses also pass. Plan on needing to pass. Of the 160 DST real estate offerings we checked in the last year's SEC Form D filings, 159 had sold only to buyers who pass, as of the filing.
Most of them were filed under SEC Rule 506(c) , part of the SEC's Regulation D. Under it, the sponsor must check that you pass. The rule lists ways to check:

- Income: your IRS forms for the last two years, such as W-2s, 1099s, K-1s or your Form 1040.

- Net worth: bank and brokerage statements from the last three months, and a credit report.

- A letter from your CPA, your lawyer, a registered broker-dealer or an SEC-registered investment adviser that says they checked.

## What does a DST cost, and what is the minimum investment?
The usual minimum is $100,000. Sales commissions are about 6 percent of the money, and the sponsor's other fees come on top. The Form D filings show only the sales commissions. The other fees are in the PPM.
The smallest amount each DST offering accepts, 156 offerings Minimum, note Offerings

$1,000 · 20 from one sponsor, wealth test only 21 offerings
$25,000 to $99,999 42 offerings
$100,000 · the most common minimum 57 offerings
$100,001 to $499,999 19 offerings
$500,000 or more 17 offerings

Of the 160 DST offerings we checked, 156 named a minimum.

### What the commission means on a $400,000 sale
Our example is the same as on our capital gains page : a Grand Strand rental bought for $250,000 and sold for $400,000, with $60,000 of depreciation taken, a gain of $186,000. A 1031 exchange into a rental or a DST puts off all of the tax. A higher-income seller owes up to about $7,100 more than the chart shows, the 3.8 percent net investment income tax .
Our $400,000 example sale, put into a DST What, detail Dollars

Tax the exchange puts off · federal and South Carolina, before the 3.8% tax $39,000
DST sales commissions on the same money · about 6% of $376,000 $23,000

What is left after selling costs, $376,000, goes into the DST. The DST's commissions come on top of those selling costs.
The sales commissions alone come to about half the tax the exchange puts off, or more, before the sponsor's other fees. You do not get the commissions back. The tax is still owed later, unless you exchange again or still own the share at your death.

## How do you get your money out of a DST?
Mostly when the trust sells its property. The sponsor's planned hold is in the PPM. The SEC filings we checked do not show it. The trust in Revenue Ruling 2004-86 was set up to end after 10 years or when its building sold, whichever came first. A DST can end for you in four ways:

### You want out early
Plan to stay in until the trust sells. DST shares cannot be resold on a public market unless the conditions of SEC Rule 144 are met. A private buyer, if you find one, decides what to pay.

### The trust sells the property
You get your share of the money. Put it into a new 1031 exchange, with new deadlines, or pay the tax.

### A REIT buys back your shares
Some DSTs are sold by large real estate companies called REITs (real estate investment trusts). After two years, the REIT may take back your shares, for cash or for units that cannot go into a later 1031 exchange, at the REIT's choice. If you get the units, your exchanges stop there. At least 13 REITs described this kind of buy-back in their latest annual reports.

### You still own it at your death
Your heirs generally take it at its value on the date of death, so the gain you put off is not taxed to them. A rental you keep until death gets the same rule, 26 U.S.C. 1014 .

## Can a DST rescue a 1031 exchange that is going wrong?
Only if the DST is on the list you name by day 45. A 1031 exchange trades real property only for other real property. Every replacement, a DST share included, must be named in writing within 45 days of the sale. A DST named as a backup can still be bought if the rental you wanted falls through.
The exchange covers less of the tax if you keep cash or the sale pays off a mortgage:

- Cash you keep. You can put part of the money into the exchange and keep the rest. The cash you keep is taxed, up to the amount of your gain.

- A mortgage the sale paid off. It counts as cash you received and is taxed the same way, unless the replacement carries as much debt or you add cash. A DST can help: your share of its loan can count toward that debt. If your rental has a mortgage, raise it with your intermediary and tax adviser before you choose a DST. We give them the closing figures.

Yes. We checked Horry County's parcel file for owners with DST in the name:

## What does Chapter3 do when you sell a Grand Strand rental for a DST?
Chapter3 sells the rental. DST shares are securities, and Chapter3 does not sell them or advise on them. The DST broker sells the share. Each step of the sale and the exchange, with what our agent does:

- Before you list You choose a qualified intermediary, the company that will hold the money during the exchange, and start talking to a DST broker. After closing you have only 45 days to name the DST. We price the rental and set the listing date so the closing falls where your plan needs it. If a tenant is in the house, the time left on the lease changes which buyers can take it.

- The sale closes The money goes to your intermediary, not to you. Your 45 and 180 days start that day. We choose a buyer who can close on the date, and give your intermediary and closing attorney the closing figures.

- By day 45 You name the DST in writing, and any backups. If you want a rental here as a backup, we find and show you choices before day 45.

- By day 180 Your share of the trust is bought. If your tax return for the year of the sale is due before day 180, that due date comes first; an extension on the return moves it later. If the backup rental here is the one you buy, we handle the purchase so it closes in time.

- The trust sells You exchange again, or pay the tax. If the next exchange is a rental on the Grand Strand, we find it.

### An owner who was done managing from far away
An agent at Chapter3 sold a tenant-occupied house for a man who had owned it for 15 years. He was moving to New York to be with his sister. He did not want to manage a rental from that distance, or have anyone else manage it. The lease had eight months left.
These are his numbers, not a promise. His cash flow was over $1,200 a month. The next owner's would be about half, because the buyer would pay higher taxes and carry a larger loan.
If no investor came, the plan was to offer the tenant a buyout, so buyers who would live in the house could bid too. The agent marketed the house to our list of investors who accept modest cash flow in an appreciating area. A cash buyer closed 13 days after the listing date.

Our net proceeds calculator shows what the sale leaves you before the exchange.

Common questions

## DST questions

### Is a DST the same as a 1031 exchange?
No. A 1031 exchange is the tax rule. A DST share is one kind of property you can buy with it.

### Is a DST a REIT?
No. A REIT is a company, and its owners hold shares in it. A DST share counts, for federal income tax, as owning part of the trust's real estate itself. Because of that, it can go into a 1031 exchange.

### How is income from a DST taxed?
For federal income tax, you are treated as owning part of the trust's real estate. Your share of the rent goes on your own return, and you deduct your share of the depreciation.

### Are you personally liable for a DST's loan?
Not in the trust the IRS ruling describes. The trust took over the property's loan, and neither the trust nor any owner is personally liable on it.

# Are Myrtle Beach condos a good investment?
By Devin Day , Operations Officer · Reviewed by Tim Nash , Broker-in-Charge · Updated October 4, 2026
Whether a Myrtle Beach condo is a good investment depends on the building: rental history, HOA dues, the master insurance policy, reserves and upcoming assessments.

The direct answer

## Are Myrtle Beach condos a good investment?
They can be excellent and they can be money pits, and the difference is almost never the unit itself. It comes down to three things: the building you buy into, the loan you can get on it, and who manages the rentals. Get those three right and a Myrtle Beach condo can outperform most coastal rental markets on price alone. Oceanfront units here still start under $200,000.
This page covers the three deciders, plus the fees and taxes that surprise first-time condo investors.

Decider one

## The building matters more than the unit
Two identical units a block apart can earn different amounts because the buildings differ: rental history, HOA dues, the master insurance policy, reserve savings, and upcoming special assessments. The right building can produce far more revenue than a nearly identical unit in the wrong one. We keep a building-by-building map of operations and fees: the oceanfront building directory .
Before any offer, we read the building's bylaws, budget, and reserve study, and we ask for its rental history. A pretty unit in a struggling building is still a bad investment.
Ask us to check a building Call 854.333.2135

Decider two

## Condotel financing limits your lender list
Many oceanfront buildings are classified as condotels: buildings that operate like hotels, with front desks and nightly rental programs. Normal conventional loans often do not work in them, which means larger down payments and fewer willing lenders. What a furnished unit can write off in its first year is on our cost segregation page .
This is where buyers lose deals, so line up financing before you shop. Our preferred lender, BrickWood Mortgage , works these buildings regularly and can tell you which ones close cleanly before you spend on an inspection. DSCR loans , which qualify on the unit's rent instead of your tax returns, are a common fit. We wrote a full guide to this: condotel financing in Myrtle Beach .

Decider three

## Do not default to the on-site property manager
Many of the best-performing condo buildings have the most aggressive and expensive on-site management companies. We see this pattern most often, and almost nobody warns buyers about it. The building earns well, the on-site manager points to that success, and owners sign up without shopping around.
Most owners would do better comparing prices and results with other local property managers before signing with the on-site company. In most buildings you are not required to use the on-site manager, though some master deeds add rules, so we confirm that document before you buy. The difference between management contracts is often the difference between a condo that pays you and one that mostly pays its manager. Rental program or Airbnb lists the fee lines to compare.

The costs

## The fees and taxes, all of them
Budget every line below before you offer. Our analyzer builds them into the projection automatically when you run an address. When it is time to exit, the sale side has its own guide: selling a condo in Myrtle Beach .

- &#10003; HOA dues. Usually include the master insurance policy and some utilities. Verify exactly what is inside the number.

- &#10003; An HO-6 policy. Your own insurance for the interior of the unit, on top of the building's master policy.

- &#10003; Special assessments. Older oceanfront buildings levy them for big repairs. The reserve study tells you the risk.

- &#10003; Property tax at 6 percent. Investment property is assessed at South Carolina's 6 percent ratio and pays the school operating tax. The bill is about 2.5 to 3.8 times an owner-occupant's on the same unit.

- &#10003; Rental taxes and licenses. Short-term rentals collect accommodations and hospitality taxes and need a business license.

- &#10003; Management and cleaning. The management split and turnover cleaning are usually the biggest line after the mortgage.

## Frequently asked questions

### Are Myrtle Beach condos a good investment?
They can be. Prices start lower than almost any coastal market and vacation demand is deep, with roughly 19 million visitors a year. The outcome depends on the building's finances and rental history, the loan you can get on it, and the management deal. Judge those three, not the countertops.

## Horry Property Tax: Why Rentals Pay 3-4x More | Chapter3
URL: https://chapter3realty.com/buyers/property-taxes/
Summary: Horry County property taxes explained: the 4% owner-occupied rate, the 6% rate on second homes and rentals, real dollar examples, and a calculator.

Home / Buyers / Property Taxes
Property taxes

# Horry County property taxes: why a rental pays three to four times more.
By Devin Day , Operations Officer · Reviewed by Tim Nash , Broker-in-Charge · Updated October 27, 2026
Horry County property taxes: live in the house and pay one of the lowest bills on the East Coast. Rent it and pay three to four times more. Calculator included.
Estimate a tax bill

The direct answer

## How South Carolina's 4% and 6% property tax rates work
Every home in Horry County falls into one of two classes. Your legal residence , the home you own and live in, is assessed at 4 percent of its value. Everything else , second homes, vacation condos, rentals, investment property, is assessed at 6 percent. Those are the official names in state law, and there is no separate "second home rate": 6 percent is simply what you pay when the home is not your legal residence. The federal count for a unit you both rent and use is a different test, on our 14-day rule page .
The ratio is only half the story. Legal residences are also fully exempt from the school operating tax, the single biggest line on a Horry County bill at 109.1 mills for 2026. Six percent properties pay all of it. Stack the two rules and the real gap is not 1.5 times. It is about 3.3 times in unincorporated Horry County and about 3.8 times inside the city of Myrtle Beach. In Conway it is about 2.5 times.
Real numbers for a $400,000 house, tax year 2026:
Location 4% legal residence 6% second home / rental
City of Myrtle Beach about $1,615 about $6,110
Unincorporated Horry County about $1,470 about $4,820

Myrtle Beach's 4 percent figure includes the city's Tourism Development Fee credit, 53.4 percent of the city tax for 2026. All figures are estimates from certified 2026 millage, before the 65-plus Homestead Exemption.

Getting the 4%

## Applying for the 4% legal residence rate in Horry County
Move into a home you own and do nothing, and Horry County bills you at 6 percent. The 4 percent legal residence rate takes an application with the county Assessor, and approval turns on proving the home is your primary residence. Planning to rent it short-term instead? Start with the short-term rental rules by city . To claim the 4 percent rate you will need:

- &#10003; SC driver's license or ID for every owner-occupant, and their spouse.

- &#10003; SC vehicle registration showing the property address.

- &#10003; Redacted tax returns , the first pages of your most recent federal 1040 and SC return.

- &#10003; One per household, nationwide. You and your spouse get one 4 percent residence between you, and you certify under penalty of perjury that you claim no other.

- &#10003; The 72-day rental rule. Rent the home more than 72 days in a calendar year and the 4 percent is gone. Fourteen days or fewer and the rental income is federal income tax free on top.

The legal window runs through January 15 of the year after the tax year, but the county asks for applications by May 31 so your October bill prints at 4 percent from the start. File once and it stays until something changes; you have six months to report a change like moving out or renting it. Relocating here? Getting the license, registration, and this application done in the right order is part of our relocation checklist .

The reset

## Why property taxes go up the year after you buy
This sequence surprises almost every new owner. Your first October bill is still calculated from the seller's assessment class and the seller's taxable value. Then, the following year, up to three resets land at once. The taxable value resets to roughly what you paid, because a sale is an "assessable transfer of interest." The ratio flips to 6 percent if the home is not your legal residence. With the 6 percent comes the full school operating tax. A bill that read $1,500 at closing becomes $5,000 or more twelve months later, and if your mortgage escrow was set from the old bill, the shortage gets collected from you on top. Inherited homes get the same reset when they leave the 4 percent class; details in our guide to selling an inherited house .
Investors get one partial break: the 25 percent ATI exemption. If the property was already taxed at 6 percent before you bought it, you can knock 25 percent off the new taxable value, with limits, by filing with the Assessor before January 31 of the first year you claim it. It is not automatic either. We flag it on every eligible purchase.
Our clients do not get the year-two surprise, because we never price a deal from the seller's old bill. Every analysis we run prices the tax at your future reality: your purchase price, the correct district millage, 6 percent if it is a rental. What still surprises people is what the honest number does to a deal. Taxes at the 6 percent rate can be the roughly $150 a month that turns a marginal rental's cash flow negative, and we would rather show you that before you offer than let the county show you after. Run any address through the Grand Investor Tool and the correct tax is already in the projection.

65 and older

## The South Carolina Homestead Exemption at age 65
Homeowners 65 or older, totally and permanently disabled, or legally blind get the first $50,000 of their legal residence's market value exempted entirely. Requirements: the home already has the 4 percent rate, one year of South Carolina residency, and you reached 65 by December 31 of the year before. In Horry County you apply in person at the Auditor's office, once; it renews on its own afterward.
On a typical bill that is another $180 to $290 a year saved, on top of a 4 percent bill that is already among the lowest of any East Coast beach market. Low carrying costs are a large part of why this area works so well on a fixed income; the full picture is on our retiring to Myrtle Beach page.

The calendar

## Horry County property tax due dates and penalties

- &#10003; Around October 1: bills mail to the owner of record.

- &#10003; January 15: last day to pay without penalty.

- &#10003; January 16 / February 2 / March 17: penalties step up 3 percent, then 10, then 15, and on March 17 the account goes delinquent and starts down the tax sale track.

- &#10003; Also separate: vehicles, boats, and RVs get their own 6 percent bills in Horry County, paid before you can register with the DMV, plus a $50 per-vehicle road fee. New residents meet these first.

Common questions

## Horry County property tax FAQ

### How much are property taxes in Myrtle Beach?
For tax year 2026, a $400,000 home in the city of Myrtle Beach pays about $1,615 a year if it is the owner's legal residence at the 4 percent rate. The same home pays about $6,100 a year at the 6 percent rate that applies to second homes and rentals. In unincorporated Horry County the same house is taxed about $1,470 at 4 percent and about $4,800 at 6 percent. The rate class matters more than the house.

### Why is the gap between the 4% and 6% rate so large?
Two reasons stack. The assessment ratio, the share of your home's value that gets taxed, is 1.5 times higher. Properties at 6 percent also pay the school operating tax, 109.1 mills in Horry County for 2026, which 4 percent legal residences are fully exempt from under Act 388. Together the real bill is about 2.5 to 3.8 times higher, depending on the town.

### How do I get the 4% legal residence rate in Horry County?
Apply with the Horry County Assessor after you move in. It is never automatic; without an approved application you are billed at 6 percent. You will need your SC driver's license or ID, SC vehicle registration at the property address, and redacted federal and state tax returns, for both spouses. The county asks for applications by May 31 so your October bill prints at the right rate. One legal residence per household, and renting the home more than 72 days a year forfeits the rate.

### Why did my property tax bill jump the year after I bought?
Your first October bill still reflects the seller's status and the seller's taxable value. The following year, three resets can hit at once. The value resets to roughly your purchase price because a sale is an assessable transfer of interest. The ratio changes to 6 percent if the home is not your legal residence, and you lose the school operating exemption with it. That is how a $1,500 bill becomes $5,000 or more. We calculate the real post-sale number for every buyer before they offer.

### Do retirees get a property tax break in South Carolina?
Yes. On top of the 4 percent rate, homeowners 65 and older, or totally disabled or legally blind, get the Homestead Exemption: the first $50,000 of the home's market value is exempt. You need one year of South Carolina residency, and in Horry County you apply in person at the Auditor's office. It renews automatically after the first application.

### Can I rent my home out and keep the 4% rate?
Only up to 72 days per calendar year. Rent it more than that and the property moves to 6 percent. Rent it 14 days or fewer and the rental income is also federal income tax free on top. Between 15 and 72 days you keep the 4 percent but owe accommodations taxes and need a business license.

## Myrtle Beach Home Insurance: What It Costs, 6 Ways to Cut It
URL: https://chapter3realty.com/buyers/coastal-insurance/
Summary: What home insurance costs on the Grand Strand: the three policies coastal owners carry, hurricane deductibles in real dollars, and how to pay less.

Home / Buyers / Coastal Insurance
Insurance on the coast

# What home insurance costs in Myrtle Beach, and six ways to lower it.
By Devin Day , Operations Officer · Reviewed by Tim Nash , Broker-in-Charge · Updated October 27, 2026
Three separate insurance policies, percentage deductibles, and flood risk the map does not show. What each one costs on the Grand Strand, and how to pay less.
Get a property's insurance costs Call 854.333.2135

The direct answer

## Average home insurance cost in Myrtle Beach
Typical single-family policies here cost about $1,500 to $3,500 a year in the standard market. National comparison sites that price one standardized $300,000 house put Myrtle Beach between about $4,500 and $5,300 a year, among the highest in South Carolina and well above the inland cities. Both numbers come from actual quotes. On the coast, quotes on the same house vary by thousands of dollars, so the person who shops wins. Premium benchmarks come from the South Carolina Department of Insurance ; check any address's flood zone free at the FEMA Map Service Center .
South Carolina home insurance rose about 10 percent in 2025, roughly double the national pace. The state insurance department attributes the pressure to repair-cost inflation, reinsurance costs, and rising home values. Reinsurance is the coverage insurers buy to protect themselves. No carrier exodus has happened here, but several national companies slowed new coastal business in 2024 and 2025, which makes shopping across many carriers matter even more.
The bigger surprise for buyers from inland states is not the price. It is that "insurance" on the coast can mean three separate policies. That is the next section.

The structure

## Homeowners, wind, and flood: the three coastal policies

- 1. Homeowners. Fire, theft, liability, the standard package. On the coast, check what it excludes before you check the price.

- 2. Wind and hail, sometimes separate. Inside the state wind pool's territory, South Carolina lets insurers exclude wind from the homeowners policy. About 1 in 6 coastal policies are written that way. Around Myrtle Beach the territory reaches inland to Carolina Bays Parkway and River Oaks Drive. The wind coverage then comes from another carrier or from the state's wind pool, the insurer of last resort. Two premiums instead of one.

- 3. Flood, always separate. No homeowners policy covers flood, anywhere, at any price. Flood coverage is its own federal or private policy. Statewide, federal flood policies average roughly $740 to $930 a year; high-risk beach and inlet properties pay well more.

Then the deductible math. Coastal policies use percentage deductibles for named storms, usually 1 to 5 percent of the dwelling coverage. On a $400,000 house, 2 percent means the first $8,000 of hurricane damage is yours. At 5 percent, $20,000. Two policies can carry the same premium and be thousands of dollars apart in a storm. We read the deductible page as well as the quote. What named storms have done here since 1989 is on our storm history page .

The flood map myth

## Myrtle Beach flood zones: Zone X does not mean no flood risk
Buyers read "Zone X" on the flood map and hear "does not flood." The map does not say that. It says the lender will not force you to buy flood insurance. FEMA's own numbers: more than 1 in 4 flood claims come from outside the high-risk zones. In Horry County, thousands more properties face real flood risk than sit inside the mapped zones that require coverage.
Two pieces of good news. Horry County's participation in the federal Community Rating System takes 25 percent off flood premiums countywide. For lower-risk homes, a flood policy is often a few hundred dollars a year, cheap insurance against the claim category most likely to surprise you.
The map also says nothing about the past. A house can sit in Zone X and still have flooded before, and sellers do not always volunteer that. We pull the flood zone on every property we show, and when the history matters, we dig for it: how to find out if a house flooded .

Rentals pay more

## Landlord and short-term rental insurance: renting changes every policy
Investment property costs more to insure , and the penalty for not telling your insurer is worse than the premium. A long-term rental needs a landlord policy, typically 15 to 25 percent above an owner-occupant policy. Short-term rental use needs coverage written for short-term rentals. Federal flood insurance charges non-primary homes a $250 annual surcharge instead of $25, with premiums allowed to rise 25 percent a year instead of 18 as rates are brought up to full risk.
An owner on the Grand Strand went through exactly this. He was moving out, buying his next home, and turning his current house into an Airbnb. When his insurance company learned the home was being rented on Airbnb, they called him and raised his flood premium by more than 25 percent. The policy was re-shopped across a network of local insurance agents, the same way it had been when he bought the house, and an agent who had not been the cheapest option the first time won the business now. His increase landed at about 10 percent instead of 25.
Two lessons. Rental use gets discovered, so declare it and price it from the start, our investment analyzer budgets the landlord premium into the cash flow. The carrier that was right for you as an owner-occupant is often not the right one for you as a landlord. Shop the change the same way you shopped the purchase.

Condos

## What condo owners pay, and why dues went up with it
A condo owner pays twice for insurance. You buy your own unit policy, commonly $40 to $60 a month here. You also pay a share of the building's master policy through your dues, and that is where the increases happened. Master policy premiums on oceanfront buildings roughly doubled or tripled between 2022 and 2025, and dues rose with them. The market has been stabilising since, with many associations finding cheaper wind coverage again, but the dues increases already happened.
Which policy pays for what is decided by the recorded master deed, not by state law, and it varies building to building. That split decides how much your own policy has to cover, whether a storm deductible can reach you, and what a lender will require. We cover the mechanism in full on condo master insurance versus your HO-6 .
Paying less

## How to lower coastal home insurance costs: six ways

- &#10003; A fortified roof, partly paid by the state. South Carolina's SC Safe Home program grants up to $7,500 toward a storm-rated roof retrofit on owner-occupied homes. Horry County owners won 294 of those grants in 2025, more than any county in the state, and grantees report premium cuts up to 24 percent. Applications open in windows, so get on the list early.

- &#10003; Wind mitigation credits. Shutters, roof straps, impact glass. State law requires insurers to tell you at every renewal which discounts exist. A wind mitigation inspection costs a couple hundred dollars and can trim the wind portion of the bill for years.

- &#10003; Deductibles you choose on purpose. Raising the named-storm percentage lowers the premium. Pair it with South Carolina's Catastrophe Savings Account, which lets you bank the deductible free of state income tax.

- &#10003; Shop through independent agents. One coastal quote is not a market. Our re-shop of that flood policy cut a 25 percent increase to 10. The state insurance department even runs a free locator service for owners who get stuck.

- &#10003; Document your elevation. For flood pricing, first-floor height matters. An elevation certificate can reprice a policy, and private flood quotes are worth comparing against the federal program.

- &#10003; Buy the right house. Roof age, construction year, elevation, and distance from the water all affect the price. We give you the insurance costs before you offer, not at closing.

## Know the Myrtle Beach insurance bill before you offer.
Send us the address. We pull the flood zone, flag wind territory, and get real quotes from our network of agents so the premium never surprises your budget. To see insurance next to taxes, dues, and the loan payment in one monthly number, use the cost to own calculator .
Call 854.333.2135 Message us

Common questions

## Myrtle Beach home insurance FAQ

### How much is homeowners insurance in Myrtle Beach?
Local single-family policies commonly cost about $1,500 to $3,500 a year in the standard market, and comparison sites quoting a standardized $300,000 house put Myrtle Beach between about $4,500 and $5,300, among the highest in South Carolina. The honest answer is a range: age of roof, distance to the ocean, deductibles, and rental use swing the number by thousands. The spread between quotes on the same house is exactly why we shop every policy across multiple agents.

### Do I need flood insurance in Myrtle Beach?
Your lender requires it only if the home sits in a FEMA high-risk zone (AE or VE). But no homeowners policy covers flood, and FEMA reports that more than 1 in 4 flood claims come from outside high-risk zones. Horry County properties get a 25 percent discount on federal flood insurance through the county's rating, and lower-risk homes often cost a few hundred dollars a year to cover. We pull the flood zone on every property before you offer.

### What is the South Carolina wind pool, and will my policy exclude wind?
Inside the state wind pool's territory, insurers are allowed to exclude wind and hail from a homeowners policy. Around Myrtle Beach that territory reaches inland to Carolina Bays Parkway and River Oaks Drive. Farther south it reaches the Intracoastal Waterway. When that happens, you buy a separate wind policy, sometimes from the state's insurer of last resort, the South Carolina Wind and Hail Underwriting Association. About 1 in 6 coastal policies are written without wind. It is not a dealbreaker, it is a second premium to budget for, and we flag it before you offer.

### What is a hurricane deductible?
Coastal policies carry a percentage deductible for named storms instead of a flat dollar amount, usually 1 to 5 percent of the dwelling coverage. On a $400,000 house, a 2 percent hurricane deductible means the first $8,000 of storm damage is yours; at 5 percent it is $20,000. Know the percentage before you buy, and consider South Carolina's Catastrophe Savings Account, which lets you set aside that deductible free of state income tax.

### Does renting my house out raise my insurance?
Yes, and hiding it is worse. A long-term rental needs a landlord policy, typically 15 to 25 percent more than a homeowner policy. Short-term rental use needs coverage written for it. Federal flood insurance also charges non-primary homes more: a $250 annual surcharge instead of $25, and premiums allowed to rise 25 percent a year instead of 18. If your insurer discovers rental use on its own, expect a repriced policy or a denied claim. Tell them, then shop the new premium hard.

### How can I lower my coastal insurance premium?
The biggest levers are a fortified roof, wind mitigation credits insurers must disclose by law, and raising deductibles you can cover. Also compare the on-site quote against multiple carriers through an independent agent, and for flood, document your elevation. South Carolina's SC Safe Home program grants up to $7,500 toward a fortified roof, and Horry County received more of those grants in 2025 than any other county. Grantees of the roof program report premium cuts up to 24 percent.

## Condotel Loans in Myrtle Beach: Most Banks Say No | Chapter3
URL: https://chapter3realty.com/invest/condotel-financing/
Summary: How to finance a condotel or non-warrantable condo in Myrtle Beach: which loans work, what down payment to expect, and why most banks say no.

Condotel and non-warrantable condo loans

# Condotel financing in Myrtle Beach: most banks say no, and the loans exist anyway.
By Devin Day , Operations Officer · Reviewed by Tim Nash , Broker-in-Charge · Updated October 27, 2026
Most banks will not finance a Myrtle Beach condotel, and the loans exist anyway: how condotel financing works, what it costs, and how to get one.
Have us check a building's financing Call 854.333.2135

The direct answer

## Can you finance a condotel in Myrtle Beach? Yes.
A condotel is a condo building that operates like a hotel: a front desk, nightly bookings, housekeeping, and units marketed to vacationers. A large share of the oceanfront buildings in Myrtle Beach work exactly this way. It is one of the most common property types in this market, and one of the hardest to finance at a normal bank.
Call a franchise lender, a big bank, or most credit unions about a condotel unit and the answer is no. Not because you are a weak borrower. Because the building fails their rules. The loans that do work are DSCR loans, portfolio loans, and other non-agency programs, and they close on the Grand Strand every week.
This page explains what makes a building a condotel or non-warrantable, why most lenders decline them, what the workable loans look like, and how to confirm a building's status before you spend money on an offer and an inspection.

The classification

## What makes a condo non-warrantable
Warrantable means a condo project passes Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac project rules, so a lender can sell the loan to them. Non-warrantable means the project fails those rules, the loan cannot be sold, and most retail lenders will not write it. Common reasons a Grand Strand building fails:

- &#10003; Hotel-style operations. A front desk, nightly and weekly rentals, central booking, or units marketed as lodging. This is the condotel trigger, and it covers much of the oceanfront.

- &#10003; Active litigation. The HOA is suing or being sued over construction or money. We wrote a full page on buying a condo in litigation .

- &#10003; Weak reserves or delinquent dues. The budget sets aside too little for repairs, or too many owners are behind on HOA payments.

- &#10003; Concentration problems. One person or company owns too many units, or too much of the building is commercial space like restaurants and shops.

- &#10003; Mandatory rental programs. The master deed requires owners to put units in the building's rental pool.

Every condotel is non-warrantable. Not every non-warrantable building is a condotel. Either way, the financing answer is the same: you need a lender that keeps the loan or sells it outside the agencies.

The loans that work

## Condotel loan requirements: down payment, rates, and terms

- &#10003; DSCR loans. The loan qualifies on the unit's rental income instead of your tax returns. This is the loan most condotel investors here end up using. Full guide: DSCR loans .

- &#10003; Portfolio and bank statement loans. Lenders that keep loans on their own books set their own project rules, so a condotel is a judgment call instead of an automatic no.

- &#10003; A substantially larger down payment than a warrantable condo. That is the realistic expectation for most programs. More down usually buys a better rate.

- &#10003; Rates a step above agency loans. The loan cannot be sold to Fannie or Freddie, so it prices higher. That part is structural and honest.

- &#10003; No FHA or VA. Those programs require approved condo projects, and condotel buildings do not qualify.

Now the part almost nobody says out loud. Because so few lenders offer condotel loans, some that do treat scarcity as a pricing strategy. They know you have nowhere else to go, so the fees grow. On an investment purchase, inflated fees come straight out of your cash flow before you collect a single night's rent.
BrickWood Mortgage , our affiliated lender, arranges condotel and non-warrantable loans through wholesale lenders that accept these buildings, and charges the same lender fees on a condotel file as on any other loan it originates, an FHA loan included. Rates and terms still depend on the building, the down payment, and the program. The fee side is simply not where you should pay extra.

A real file

## A Myrtle Beach condotel purchase, after a year of lender declines
A buyer in the area came in as a referral. He and his agent had both been calling lenders separately, looking for anyone who would finance the condotel unit he wanted to buy. Bank after bank, franchise lender after franchise lender, the answer was the same no, on a property type this market sells thousands of.
BrickWood financed the unit at its standard fees, the same fee structure an FHA borrower pays. The purchase closed. His agent noticed. Both of them have kept sending condotel purchases the same way since, because they know the building will not stop the loan and the fees will not rise because the word condotel appeared in the file.
Condotel loans are not a premium specialty product. They are normal loans at a lender that does them all the time.

## Condotel financing FAQ

### Can you get a mortgage on a condotel in Myrtle Beach?
Yes. Most banks, credit unions, and franchise lenders will decline the building, but condotels close every week here through DSCR loans, portfolio loans, and other non-agency programs. Expect a larger down payment than a standard condo asks, and confirm the building with a lender before you write an offer.

### What is the difference between a condotel and a non-warrantable condo?
A condotel is a condo building run like a hotel: front desk, nightly bookings, and units marketed as lodging. Non-warrantable is the broader lending label for any condo project that fails those rules, which includes condotels plus buildings with active litigation, low reserves, too much commercial space, or one owner holding too many units. Every condotel is non-warrantable, but not every non-warrantable building is a condotel.

### What down payment does a condotel loan require?
Plan on a substantially larger down payment than a standard condo loan for most condotel and non-warrantable programs, and putting still more down buys stronger pricing. Exact requirements depend on the lender, the building, and whether the unit is a second home or an investment.

### Can I use an FHA or VA loan to buy a condotel?
No. FHA and VA loans require the condo project to be on their approved lists, and condotel buildings do not qualify. If you want FHA or VA financing on the Grand Strand, you will be shopping standard condo buildings or single-family homes instead.

### Do condotel loans cost more than regular condo loans?
Often, and more than they should. Because so few lenders offer the product, some that do treat it as a premium service and pad the fees, which hurts your cash flow from day one. Rates are higher than agency condo loans because the loan cannot be sold to Fannie or Freddie, but the lender fees do not have to be inflated. BrickWood Mortgage charges the same lender fees on a condotel file as on any other loan it originates.

Ask a lender to review the project before you write the offer, not after. We keep current information on which Grand Strand buildings close cleanly and which ones need a specialty loan. Send us the building name and we will tell you what financing it takes.

The direct answer

## What HOA fees pay for, and why they vary so much
An HOA fee, called a regime fee on many South Carolina condos, is what every owner pays to run the shared parts of the property. That association's budget sets what the fee buys, and it varies enormously.
On an oceanfront condo the dues typically carry the building's master insurance, the roof and exterior, elevators, pools, trash, pest control, and often water, sewer and cable. That is why oceanfront dues run high: coastal windstorm insurance and salt-air maintenance are expensive, and the building is buying them for you. On an inland single-family HOA the dues may cover a pool, an entrance and some landscaping, and nothing else.
The useful comparison is never dues against dues. It is dues against what they include, plus what the association has saved for the repairs it has not made yet.

The local reality

## Horry County leads South Carolina in HOA complaints
This is not an impression. The South Carolina Department of Consumer Affairs publishes an annual HOA complaint report because state law requires it. In the 2026 report, covering 2025, Horry County accounted for 31 percent of every HOA complaint filed in the state , more than any other county, and led the state per capita at 0.38 complaints per 1,000 residents. Georgetown County was second per capita.
Statewide, HOA complaints rose 176 percent between 2019 and 2025. The three most common issues were failure to follow or enforce the recorded rules and bylaws, maintenance and repair disputes, and requests to see association documents being ignored.
None of that means associations here are bad. It means you want someone who has read a lot of these before. Newer agents struggle to steer a buyer to the right community simply because they have not seen enough of them. We have.

Common questions

## Myrtle Beach HOA fees FAQ

### What do HOA fees cover in Myrtle Beach?
It depends entirely on the association. On a Grand Strand condo, dues often carry the building's master insurance, exterior and roof maintenance, elevators, pools, trash, pest control, and frequently water, sewer and cable. On a single-family HOA they may cover only common areas and a pool. The only way to know is to read that association's budget.

### Are low HOA fees a good sign?
Not by themselves. Low dues usually mean the association provides fewer services and covers fewer utilities. They can also mean the association is underfunding its reserves, which shows up later as a special assessment. Compare what the dues include before you compare the dues.

### Why are Horry County HOA complaints so high?
Horry County files more HOA complaints than any other county in South Carolina. In the state's 2026 report it accounted for 31 percent of all complaints and led the state per capita at 0.38 per 1,000 residents. Georgetown County was second per capita. Dense condo and planned-community development in a fast-growing coastal market is the likely driver.

### Can I refuse to join an HOA?
No. If the property is inside an association, membership and assessments run with the land. You agree to them when you buy. That is why reading the governing documents before you make an offer matters so much.

### Is there a state agency that oversees South Carolina HOAs?
No one, in the sense most owners expect. The South Carolina Department of Consumer Affairs collects HOA complaints because the law requires it, and publishes an annual report. But it does not administer or enforce the Homeowners Association Act, and its complaint process is voluntary mediation. It cannot force an association to participate or require any outcome.

### Do I get the HOA documents before I buy?
You should, and most buyers do not. In the state's 2026 report only 32 percent of complainants said they received the governing documents before purchase, while 53 percent got them after. Reading them first is the purpose of the review we run.

# Condo special assessments on the Grand Strand.
By Devin Day , Operations Officer · Reviewed by Tim Nash , Broker-in-Charge · Updated October 28, 2026
A special assessment is a charge for money the association does not have. What triggers one on the Grand Strand, how to spot it early, and who pays at resale.
Have us check a building before you offer Call 854.333.2135

The direct answer

## What a special assessment is
Regular dues cover the running of the property. A special assessment is what happens when something costs more than the association has saved: a roof, an elevator, structural repair, a jump in the master insurance premium, or litigation.
The board levies it on every unit, usually as a lump sum or over a set number of months. On a coastal condo building it can run into the thousands per unit. It is not optional, and it does not care that you only just bought.

What causes them

## What triggers a special assessment here

- &#10003; Deferred maintenance coming due. Roofs, elevators, balconies, siding. Salt air shortens the life of everything on this coast.

- &#10003; Master insurance. Coastal windstorm premiums have risen sharply. When the premium jumps mid-year and the budget cannot absorb it, the difference is assessed.

- &#10003; Structural and safety repairs. Scrutiny of condo building safety tightened across the country after 2021, and inspections now surface work that was previously deferred.

- &#10003; Litigation. Legal costs the association did not budget for.

- &#10003; Reserves that were never funded. The most common underlying cause, and the most visible in advance. See reserves and reserve studies .

Seeing it coming

## How to spot one before you make an offer
A special assessment is almost never a surprise to the board. It is only a surprise to the buyer who did not read.

- &#10003; Board meeting minutes, 12 to 24 months. This is the single best document. A coming assessment gets discussed, priced and argued over for months before anyone is billed.

- &#10003; The reserve study against the building's age. If the roof has eight years left and the reserve has a fraction of what a roof costs, you are looking at the assessment already.

- &#10003; The current budget. If the association only just breaks even each year, there is nothing to spare when something goes wrong.

- &#10003; Recent dues history. Several years of flat dues in a period of rising insurance costs is not good news. It usually means the shortfall is waiting.

Who pays

## Who owes it when the unit sells
The general expectation is that an assessment already charged before closing belongs to the seller, and one charged afterwards belongs to the buyer. But that is a contract term, not a law of nature, and the line gets blurry when an assessment has been approved but not yet billed.
Two things protect you. Put the allocation in the contract in writing, and get an estoppel or resale statement from the association confirming what is owed on that unit as of closing. If you are selling, the same document protects you from a charge appearing after you have gone. Related reading: selling a condo in Myrtle Beach .

Common questions

## Special assessment FAQ

### What is a condo special assessment?
A one-time charge on top of regular dues, charged when the association needs money it does not have. Roofs, elevators, structural repair, an insurance shortfall or litigation are the usual causes. It is billed per unit, and it can be thousands of dollars.

### Who pays a special assessment when a condo sells?
It depends on when it was charged and what the contract says. An assessment already voted and charged before closing is normally the seller's, but that is a contract term, not an automatic rule. Get it in writing, and get an estoppel or resale statement from the association confirming what is owed.

### How can I tell if a special assessment is coming?
Read the last twelve to twenty-four months of board meeting minutes, the reserve study, and the budget. Minutes are where a coming assessment is discussed long before it is charged. Thin reserves against an aging roof or elevator is the classic setup.

### Can a special assessment stop my loan?
It can. Lenders review a condo project as well as the borrower, and an unresolved assessment tied to safety, structural or habitability repairs can make the whole building ineligible for a conventional loan. Our non-warrantable condos page explains that review.

### Can I refuse to pay a special assessment?
Not realistically. A properly charged assessment is a debt on the unit and can become a lien. If you believe it was charged improperly, that is a question for a South Carolina attorney, not something to settle by withholding payment.

# Can a Myrtle Beach condo association pay for its own roof? Its reserve fund tells you. South Carolina law does not require one.

- 56% of condos for sale are in buildings 30+ years old

By Devin Day , Operations Officer · Reviewed by Tim Nash , Broker-in-Charge · Updated November 1, 2026
A Myrtle Beach condo's roof and elevators wear out on a schedule. If its reserves cover the worn part, it can pay. If not, the owners do.

The short answer
Only if it has saved enough. To tell, compare the cash in its reserve fund with what its reserve study says the fund should hold by now. That share is called percent funded. The higher it is, the lower the chance the owners get a special assessment.

## What is an HOA reserve fund?
A reserve fund is money a homeowners association (HOA) or condo association saves each year for big repairs it knows are coming. The roof, the elevators and the paving are the usual ones.

- Account 1 The operating budget Pays this year's bills, from this year's dues.

- Account 2 The reserve fund Saves for the big repairs ahead: the roof, the elevators, the paving.

- When the reserve is short The owners Pay the rest, often as a special assessment .

Saving ahead spreads the cost of a roof across every owner who uses it. Without savings, the whole bill falls on whoever owns a unit the year the roof fails.
A reserve study is a report on the building's big shared parts: what each one costs, how long it lasts, and how much the fund should hold by now.

## Does South Carolina require HOA reserves or a reserve study?
No. South Carolina law does not require a condo or an HOA to keep a reserve fund, to put any amount into one, or to have a reserve study. How much a building saves is up to its board and its own documents.
In a South Carolina condo, every owner shares the cost of keeping up and repairing the shared parts. Each unit's share is the percentage set for it in the condo's founding papers, the recorded documents that created it. After damage, the bill is paid in this order:

- Insurance Pays first, for what the master policy covers.

- The reserve fund Pays next, from what the board has saved.

- The owners Share the rest, by each unit's percentage in the founding papers.

A condo board must keep a book of every receipt and expense, with repair costs shown, open to every owner. A buyer is not yet an owner, so we get the papers through the seller.

## How much should a Myrtle Beach condo association have in reserves?
Enough to cover the part of each big repair that has already worn out. A roof halfway through its life should have about half its cost saved.
Percent funded: what the fund holds, against what it should hold
Association Reserves, a national reserve-study firm, set these bands from its clients' studies. The two marks are the example building below, with less and with more saved.
In the weak band, repairs are often put off. In the strong band, the risk of a special assessment is low, and a fund does not need to be full to get there.
Among the firm's own clients, about a third were weak and a quarter strong. Those are associations that pay for a study, and the firm says they may be more careful with money than most.
Percent funded is a snapshot of today. It does not grade the plan, so we read the plan as well.

## What does an underfunded condo building look like?
Here is one building with round numbers. It has 80 units, is 30 years old and has $400,000 saved.

- 2 Elevator machinery, two elevators 17 of 20 years used

- 3 Exterior paint 6 of 8 years used

The flat roof, the elevator machinery and the exterior paint come due. By then the fund will hold about two thirds of what they cost.

The same building at 75 percent funded has no gap. The concrete balconies come next, 10 years out.
The example leaves out inflation and interest. A real condo splits a gap by each unit's percentage in its founding papers, not evenly.

### Saving ahead costs owners less
Saved money earns interest. A special assessment pays the full price, and a bank loan adds its interest.
What a $250,000 roof costs the owners, three ways How it is paid, why cost to owners

Saved for ahead · less than the price: savings earn interest $230,000
A special assessment · the full price, all at once $250,000
A bank loan · plus the interest on the loan $320,000

The same reserve-study firm's example, rounded to the nearest $10,000.

## What do lenders require for condo reserves?
For most conventional condo loans, the lender tests the building's budget. Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac buy these loans from lenders, and the test is theirs.

- How a building passes At least 10 percent of its dues goes into reserves. Or it saves what a current reserve study says it should.

- When it fails A buyer there cannot get a conventional loan that follows these rules, though some other loans still work. When you sell a condo there, your buyer's lender runs the same test.

### 10 percent or 15 percent?
Freddie Mac raises its line to 15 percent for loan applications received on or after January 4, 2027. It says it made the change with its regulator and in alignment with Fannie Mae. Fannie Mae's own guide still says 10 percent.
From that date, a building that puts 12 percent into reserves fails Freddie Mac's test and passes Fannie Mae's guide as it reads now. Which one applies depends on which company buys your loan. Your loan officer can tell you before you apply.
Freddie Mac made the change after buildings with underfunded reserves turned out to be the same ones needing critical repairs. It says owners in those buildings can face special assessments or higher dues.

### A building can pass and still be weak
The test reads one line of this year's budget, not the cash in the bank. Our example building puts 10.4 percent of its dues into reserves, so it passes while 26 percent funded. Try your own building's numbers:
Does this budget pass the lender's test?

The HOA fee will not tell you which condo buildings have saved. In buildings 30 years or older, the middle listed fee is about $700 a month, close to the $640 for all condos for sale. We read the study instead.

## What do other states require for condo reserves?
Florida , New Jersey , Maryland and Virginia make condo boards study their reserves on a schedule. A buyer from one of them should not expect the same here.
What the law requires of condo associations, by state
State Reserve study required How often
South Carolina No Never required
Florida Yes, for condo buildings 3 stories or taller At least every 10 years
New Jersey Yes At least every 5 years for concrete, masonry or steel condo buildings
Maryland Yes At least every 5 years
Virginia Yes, unless the condo's own papers say otherwise At least every 5 years

## What if a building has no reserve study, or an old one?
No law here requires a reserve study, so a building can have none, or one that is years old. A missing study is a reason to look harder, not proof of a problem.
Without one, we judge the building from its budget, its balance sheet, its board minutes and the age of its big parts.
When there is a study, a lender accepts it, or an update, only if it is no more than three years old. Among the same reserve-study firm's clients, associations that update at least every three years were told to charge a new special assessment about half as often as those that update every five.

## What should a buyer check in a condo's reserves?
Our agents read the HOA documents for a buyer. For reserves, these five tell us whether the building can pay for its own roof:

- The reserve study. Its date, the percent funded and its plan. A plan that only keeps the fund above zero is a warning.

- The budget's reserve line. The share of the dues it puts into reserves.

- The balance sheet. The cash in reserves, against what the study says should be there.

- The age of the big parts. The roof, the elevators, the paint and the balconies, against HUD's lives and the year the building was built.

- The board's minutes. Repairs put off, or a special assessment under discussion. The HOA documents a buyer receives are only part of what we ask for.

What you get when we read a building
Its percent funded, its cash against the study, whether its budget passes a lender's test, and the big parts coming due.
Send us the building's name

### When you see the papers, and when you can still back out

- Before you sign In most resales, the seller fills in a disclosure form. It asks whether the association has levied any special assessments.

- After you sign The standard South Carolina sales contract has a due diligence period. In it, you can end the contract with a written notice to the seller.

- Inside that period Read the reserve study, the budget, the balance sheet and the minutes.

If they are weak, you can ask for a lower price or a credit at closing, or walk away.

Common questions

## Reserve questions

### Does South Carolina require a reserve study?
No, and it requires no reserve fund either. A board can still choose to get one, and a lender can accept a current study in place of its budget test.

### Who pays a special assessment voted before closing?
The purchase contract decides, so it belongs in the offer. A bill the seller already owes is paid at closing, and a buyer can be held to it only up to the association's written statement of it.

### Can I see an HOA's reserve records before I buy?
Members can. An HOA member can inspect and copy the budget and the accounting records after giving written notice five business days ahead. A buyer is not yet a member, so we ask the seller for them.

### Does a newer condo building need strong reserves?
A newer building needs less saved by now. A building finished in 2015 is 11 years old, short of HUD's planning life for its elevator machinery and its flat roof, so less of each has worn out. Percent funded still applies: what the fund holds against that smaller amount.

## What to Look for in HOA Documents Before Buying | Chapter3
URL: https://chapter3realty.com/hoa/documents/

What to ask for, and what each one tells you

# Reading HOA documents before you buy.
By Devin Day , Operations Officer · Reviewed by Tim Nash , Broker-in-Charge · Updated October 28, 2026
Most Grand Strand buyers see the HOA documents after they own the property. Reading them first avoids the easiest mistake there is.

The direct answer

## Most buyers read them too late
In the South Carolina Department of Consumer Affairs 2026 HOA report, only 32 percent of the homeowners who filed a complaint said they had received the governing documents before they bought . Fifty-three percent received them afterwards.
That is an agent failure, plainly. Getting those documents in front of a buyer before they are committed is the agent's job, and most of the time it does not happen. People are not breaking rules they disagreed with. They are discovering rules nobody showed them, after the obligations already came with the house.
The fix is unglamorous: get the documents early, and have someone who reads them for a living tell you what is in them.
Want us to look at it for you?
Have us review the documents Call 854.333.2135

The list

## What to ask for, and what each one reveals

- &#10003; Declaration or master deed. This is the founding document, recorded at the county. It is what legally creates the association, defines what you own versus what everybody shares, and sets the promises attached to the property itself. Those promises transfer to you at closing whether or not you read them, and you cannot negotiate them away. If you only read one document, read this one.

- &#10003; Bylaws. How the association is run: the board, voting, meetings, how rules get made and changed.

- &#10003; Rules and regulations. The day-to-day list. Pets, parking, rentals, exterior changes. Usually the easiest for a board to change, so read the minutes too.

- &#10003; Budget, balance sheet and income statement. These show what the association takes in, what it spends, and what it has saved. You are checking whether it can pay for the repairs that are coming without charging you extra later. See reserves .

- &#10003; Reserve study. What is coming and whether it is funded.

- &#10003; Board minutes, 12 to 24 months. The most underused document. Assessments, disputes and rule changes appear here first.

- &#10003; Master insurance certificate. What the building covers and what you must insure yourself. Related: coastal insurance costs .

- &#10003; Litigation disclosure. Active litigation can affect both financing and value. See buying a condo in litigation .

- &#10003; Estoppel or resale statement. What is owed on that unit right now, including any special assessment .

How we read them

## What we are looking for
We read the financials to see whether the association can pay for what is coming. Then we read the rules against how you told us you want to live.
A document review is not a legal opinion, and if something in the declaration needs a lawyer's reading we will say so. We tell you what the documents say, what it will mean for you, and which parts argue against the purchase.

Common questions

## HOA documents FAQ

### What HOA documents should I get before buying?
The declaration or master deed, the bylaws, and the current rules and regulations. This year's budget, the balance sheet and income statement, and the most recent reserve study. Board meeting minutes for the last twelve to twenty-four months. The master insurance certificate and any litigation disclosure. An estoppel or resale statement showing what is owed on the unit.

### When do I get the HOA documents?
Usually during your due diligence period, and often later than is useful. In South Carolina's 2026 HOA report only 32 percent of complainants said they received the governing documents before purchase, while 53 percent received them after. Ask for them as early as possible and treat slow delivery as information.

### Which document has the rules I have to follow?
Usually three. The declaration or master deed creates the obligations that run with the property, the bylaws govern how the association operates, and the rules and regulations are the day-to-day list that the board can change most easily.

### What are the biggest red flags in HOA documents?
Thin reserves against aging components, several years of flat dues while costs rose, active litigation, a high share of unpaid assessments, a large single owner, and restrictions that conflict with how you plan to use the property.

### Does the seller have to tell me there is an HOA?
Yes. South Carolina's residential property condition disclosure requires a seller to disclose that the property is governed by a homeowners association. That disclosure does not tell you what the rules say. That is why the documents matter.

## Myrtle Beach HOA Rental Restrictions | Chapter3 Realty
URL: https://chapter3realty.com/hoa/rental-restrictions/
Summary: What HOA recorded rules can restrict on the Grand Strand: rentals, pets, parking, porches and home businesses, and why they are separate from city laws.

Home / HOA Guide / Rules and Restrictions
Rentals, pets, parking and home businesses

# HOA rental and lifestyle restrictions.
By Devin Day , Operations Officer · Reviewed by Tim Nash , Broker-in-Charge · Updated October 28, 2026
The recorded HOA rules decide whether you can rent a Grand Strand property, for how long, and to whom. Private rules, separate from city law, that most buyers never read.
Have us check the rules before you offer Call 854.333.2135

The direct answer

## Two sets of rules control whether you can rent it out
Two different sets of rules control whether you can rent a place out, and you need both to say yes.
One is the city or county law. That decides whether short-term renting is allowed at that address at all. Those are public laws passed by local government, and they are the same for everyone in that area. We cover them on our short-term rental rules page .
The other is your community's own set of rules. When a neighborhood or condo building is created, the developer records a set of rules at the county office. Every owner is bound by them, and they transfer to you when you buy. These are private rules, not government laws, and they can be stricter than the city allows.
The city can say short-term rentals are fine at your address, and your community can still ban them completely. Neither one cancels the other. If the community says no, the answer is no, and the city permit you were counting on is worthless.

Rentals

## What HOA rental rules can stop you doing

- &#10003; Minimum lease terms. A 30-day, six-month or twelve-month minimum quietly ends any short-term rental plan.

- &#10003; Caps on the number of rentals. A limit on how many units may be leased at once, often with a waiting list. Also affects financing, since owner-occupancy ratios feed into warrantability .

- &#10003; Waiting periods. Some communities require you to own, or to live there, for a period before you may rent at all.

- &#10003; Board approval of tenants. Applications, screening, fees.

- &#10003; Outright bans. Some communities simply do not permit leasing.

A real file

## The buyer whose business plan was in the bylaws
A friend of ours was relocating to the Grand Strand to start a property management company. He planned to run it from a home office at the house he was buying.
When that community's bylaws were read, there was a restriction that would have fined him for operating the business from the property, down to registering it at that address. He had no idea. Nobody had asked him what he intended to do with the house, so nobody had thought to check.
He was told what the bylaws said, and he bought in a different community that permitted it. The house he originally wanted was a perfectly good house. It was just the wrong house for him, and the only way to know that was to read the rules against his actual plan.
Have us check the rules before you offer Call 854.333.2135

Everything else

## The rules people do not expect
Recorded rules reach much further than most buyers assume. Commonly they cover the number, size or breed of pets, and where and what you may park, including boats and work vehicles. They also cover exterior changes and paint colors, what may be left on a porch or patio, fencing, landscaping, signage, and how long a garage door may stand open.
None of that makes associations bad. Plenty of our clients specifically want a community that enforces its standards, and those communities are often the best maintained. The rules should match how you live, and you can only know that if someone reads them against your plans before you are committed.

Rentals, pets, a boat, a home office. We check the recorded rules against what you intend to do.

Common questions

## HOA rules and restrictions FAQ

### Can an HOA stop me renting my property?
Yes. An association's recorded rules can set minimum lease terms, cap how many units may be rented at once, require a waiting period before a new owner may rent, require board approval of tenants, or ban short-term rentals entirely. These are private restrictions and they are separate from city and county rental laws.

### Are HOA rental rules the same as the city short-term rental rules?
No, and you must satisfy both. City and county laws decide where short-term rentals are permitted at all. The association's recorded rules decide whether your particular community allows it. A property can be legal under the law and still prohibited by the HOA.

### Can an HOA restrict a home business?
Commonly, yes. Many declarations restrict a lot to residential use and prohibit commercial or business activity. Depending on the wording that can reach client visits, signage, deliveries, employees, and sometimes using the address as a registered business location. If you plan to work from home in any visible way, this clause needs reading before you offer.

### Can an HOA tell me how many pets I can have?
Yes. Pet limits by number, size or breed are among the most common recorded rule restrictions, along with parking, exterior changes, and what may be left on a porch or patio. These are enforceable when they are properly adopted and recorded.

### What happens if the HOA adds a rental restriction after I buy?
It depends on how the documents allow amendments and whether existing owners are grandfathered. Some amendments exempt current owners, some do not. If you are buying specifically to rent, this is a question to settle before closing, not after.

## Can an HOA Foreclose in South Carolina? Liens and Unpaid Dues
URL: https://chapter3realty.com/hoa/liens-and-foreclosure/
Summary: Yes, through the court. How a South Carolina HOA lien and foreclosure work, how often it happens in Horry County, and what stops it before the sale.

Home / HOA Guide / Liens and Foreclosure
HOA Guide

# Can an HOA take your house in South Carolina over unpaid dues? Yes, through the court, and the bill that starts it can be small.

- 4 of 19 of one month's Horry County foreclosures were for HOA or condo debts

- 89% of one South Carolina HOA's court bill was lawyers' fees and court costs

By Devin Day , Operations Officer · Reviewed by Tim Nash , Broker-in-Charge · Updated November 2, 2026
How an association forecloses, how often it happens in Horry County, and the steps that stop it before the sale.

The short answer
Yes. For a house or a condo, a South Carolina homeowners association (HOA) or condo association can put a lien on your home for unpaid dues and ask a court to sell it. The lien is on the home itself, so it applies whether or not you have a mortgage.
The bill that starts it can be small. Lawyers' fees and court costs are added to it.
If you are sued, you usually have 30 days to answer; the summons gives the time. Answer, and get the case itself dismissed, because paying the bill does not by itself end the lawsuit. Or sell before the auction.

## Can an HOA foreclose on your house in South Carolina?
Yes, for a house or a condo, through the court. An association cannot sell your home on its own. It files a lawsuit, and a judge orders the sale, the same way a bank forecloses a mortgage. It can also sue you for the money alone, without asking to sell the home.
The power comes from one of two places:

- Condo association South Carolina's condo law Unpaid dues are a lien on the unit by law, and the association can foreclose it in court.

- HOA that is not a condo The community's recorded rules These are the rules filed with the county. Courts enforce them like a contract. A lien under them is enforced through the court too.

In a 2019 case , the community's rules allowed foreclosure, and the South Carolina Supreme Court said the HOA had the legal right to foreclose. It still set that sale aside.
For an HOA that is not a condo, the state's HOA law says nothing about late fees, interest, liens or foreclosure. Those rules are in your community's own papers, so they differ from one community to the next. Our guide to South Carolina HOA law has what the state does say, and our guide to HOA violations and fines covers fines.

Associations bring a real share of the county's foreclosures, mostly against condo units. We read every case on Horry County's sale list for one month and matched each association case to the county's parcel records.
